REPORT
The Action Taken Report of the Committee deals with the action taken by the Ministry of Law
and Justice on the recommendations/observations of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing
Committee on Personnel, Public Grievances, Law and Justice in its Eighty-fourth Report on the Demands
for Grants (2016-17) of the Ministry. The Report was presented to Rajya Sabha and laid on the Table
of Lok Sabha on the 26th April, 2016.
2. The Action Taken Replies of Legislative Department, Department of Legal Affairs, Department of
Justice, Ministry of Law and Justice in respect of the recommendations contained in the above mentioned
Report were received on 8th September, 5th October and 7th November, 2016, respectively. Replies of
the Departments have been categorised as follows:
CHAPTER-I: The recommendations/observations which have been accepted by the Ministry i.e.,
in respect of paras 3.8, 3.11, 3.15, 3.19, 3.20, 3.21, 4.5, 4.10, 4.27, 4.30, 6.13,
6.15, 6.36, 6.45 and 6.53 of the Report. The Committee is pleased to note that the
Ministry has accepted its recommendations.
CHAPTER-II: The recommendations/observations which the Committee does not desire to pursue
in view of the replies given by the Ministry i.e., in respect of paras 5.7, 5.10, 4.18,
4.19, 6.14, 6.50, 6.63 and 6.64 of the Report. The Committee has accepted the
explanations furnished by the Ministry and does not wish to pursue them further
as of now.
CHAPTER-III: The recommendations/observations in respect of which Committee has not accepted
replies given by the Ministry i.e., with regard to paras 6.10, 6.59, 6.60, 6.65, 6.66
and 4.34 of the Report. The Committee expresses its concern for not accepting the
recommendations of the Committee dealt with in Chapter - III of this Report and
reiterates its recommendations.
CHAPTER-IV: The recommendations/observations on which final replies of the Ministry of Law
and Justice have not been received. The Committee desires that Ministry should
furnish action taken report in respect of recommendations mentioned in Chapter -
IV without any further delay.
3. The recommendations/observations of the Committee in its Eighty-fourth Report, the ATRs furnished
by the Ministry and the Committee's further recommendations/observations have been dealt with in the
succeeding Chapters.

ELECTION COMMISSION OF INDIA
Recommendations/Observations
2.0. The Committee appreciates the work of Election Commission of India in checking bogus voting
by electoral roll purification by linking it with Aadhar card. The Committee feels that a common
electoral roll will reduce cost, time and check electoral malpractices in the country. The Committee,
2

3
therefore, recommends that a common electoral roll be prepared in the country which can be used
from panchayat level to Parliamentary elections with the State Election Commissions, to weed out
multiple electoral rolls to check corrupt practices during elections. The Committee also recommends
the ECI to ensure that no persons voting rights are hampered by wrongfully categorizing them as
Doubtful voters as it will go against the very principle of electoral democracy. (Para 3.19)
Action Taken
2.1. The Commission is grateful to the Parliamentary Standing Committee for their appreciation. The
Commission, with the objective of making electoral rolls error free and authenticated to the extent
possible, had launched a comprehensive programme which includes feeding and seeding of Aadhar
number in electoral database under the banner "National Electoral Rolls Purification and Authentication
Programme (NERP AP), 2015" with effect from 03.03.2015.
2.2. When the activities of the programme were at its climax and some of the activities of the
programme were towards its culmination, all further activities relating to collection/feeding/seeding of
Aadhar number under NERPAP, 2015 were kept in abeyance w.e.f.13.08.2015 in pursuance of the interim
order of the Hon'ble Supreme Court dated 11.08.2015 in WP © 494 of 2012 relating to Aadhar.
2.3. So far as common electoral roll is concerned, it is stated that the Commission prepares electoral
rolls for elections to the Parliamentary and Assembly constituencies. The State Election Commissions
prepare electoral rolls for local bodies' elections. The electoral rolls for the Territorial Assembly and
Parliamentary Constituencies are prepared under the provisions of Sections 13D and 15 of the Representation
of the People Act, 1950 and enabling rules contained in the Registration of Electors Rules, 1960. The
responsibility of preparation of electoral rolls of panchayats/local bodies' elections rests with the State
Election Commission of the State concerned under Articles 243 K and 243 ZA of the Constitution of
India.
2.4. The Election Commission of India has been receiving requests from several State Election
Commissions from time to time to evolve a software for preparing common electoral rolls for local body
election and Assembly/Parliamentary elections.
2.5. Preparation of common electoral rolls involves the following issues:
(i) There is no uniform system for preparation of rolls by SEC in all States.
(ii) Present database control tables pertaining to the ECI have the particulars of administrative
units of rural and urban area, extent of assembly/parliamentary constituency, elector's details
as well as EPIC details. Fields, table name and description of tables are already fixed. These
control tables are populated and updated before any change in the existing database of the
rolls.
(iii) Sections details within polling stations under a constituency needs to be prepared as per
extent of the ward area of Panchayat and Municipal Council Elections.

4
(iv) Delimitation of Panchayat and Municipal Council wards is done frequently at the time of
elections or after every census. Whereas, change in the extent of assembly constituency
take place after 25-30 years.
(v) Even, collection of information about the ward No. and name from the existing electors
would not serve the purpose as in many cases electors themselves may not be able to
indicate such details for want of knowledge, since number and name of ward keeps on
changing very frequently.
(vi) W ard numbers are not available in some rural and urban areas in many States and different
states uses different system of nomenclature and numbering.
(vii) The additional columns in the elector's database can be created, however it will not be
possible for the ECI to collect the data of panchayat, municipal body and ward number and
feed it in the database. It is difficult for the Commission to undertake such massive exercise
for all the 78 crore electors in the country.
2.6. The Election Commission of India has issued instructions to the Chief Electoral Officers of all the
States/UTs vide Commission's letter No. 23/SEC/2008/ERS, dated 10th December, 2008 to share the
computerized electoral database with the State Election Commissions so that they could generate electoral
rolls according to the extent of their panchayat / local body wards from the same database. The terms
and conditions for sharing of electoral roll database have also been specified.
2.7. Further, The Commission vide its letter No. 23/SEC/2011-ERS, dated 3rd January, 2012, had also
provided for sharing of the ECI database with additional columns of details of ward level. However, it
is to be provided on 'as is where is' basis and additional blank columns for Panchayat, Municipal bodies
are added by the CEO, on request of SEC. However, collection and subsequent addition/modification/
updating of the data is required to be done by the concerned State Election Commissions.
2.8. The Commission in 1999 has sent a proposal to the Government regarding use of common
electoral rolls at elections conducted by the ECI and the State Election Commission (SEC). The local
bodies elections are conducted by SEC according to their own state laws. In those laws, there is no
uniform law or procedure for preparing the electoral rolls for local bodies' elections. Some States adopt
the rolls prepared by the ECI while a few States prepare the rolls separately. This not only creates
confusion among the electors because their names may be present in one roll but absent in the other,
or vice versa, but also results in duplication of efforts and expenditure. The Commission proposed that
local laws of the States should be amended to provide that electoral rolls prepared by the Commission
will be used for local bodies elections with necessary modifications/re-arrangement. This will simplify
the process of preparation of rolls and also avoid unnecessary expenditure. This was also reiterated in
2004.
2.9. The Law Commission in its Two Hundred and Fifty-fifth Report on Electoral Reforms under
chapter XVII has also endorsed the Commission's proposal. It has suggested that introducing common
electoral rolls will require an amendment in the State laws pertaining to the conduct of local body
elections, the Central Government should write to the various States in this regard.

Recommendations/Observations
3.0. The Committee recommends to the ECI to consolidate all the guidelines into a simplified 'code'
and publish the same for the knowledge of all the stakeholders. It has been observed that 'Citizens'
and their family members are often harassed by stopping their vehicle and their privacy is also
eroded in the name of implementation of the electoral code of conduct despite there being no
evidence of any illegal activity. This calls for abundant precaution on the part of implementing
agencies. (Para 3.20)
Action taken/proposed to be taken
3.1. The Commission compiles all the guidelines/instructions/advisories issued on Code of Conduct
from time to time. In continuation to this task, the Commission has already compiled the guidelines/
instructions/advisories issued till August, 2015 and published the same under the heading "Compendium
of Instructions on Model Code of Conduct". For wide dissemination of these guidelines/instructions/
advisories, the said Compendium of Instructions is also available on Commission's website under the
hyperlink-http://eci.nic.in/eci_main/ElectoralLaws/compendium/MCC_Compendium 040_92015.pdf
3.2. Regarding question of citizens and their family members often being harassed by stopping their
vehicles and their privacy being eroded, it is stated that the Commission vide its letter No. 76/Instructions/
EEPS/2015/V ol.II, dated 29th May, 2015 issued Standard Operating Procedure (SOP) for seizure and
release of cash and other items during election process and also held that no inconvenience to common
public and genuine person should be caused during checking and Flying Squads and State Surveillance
Teams shall be polite, decent and courteous, while checking the baggage or vehicle. For transparency
and accountability, each instance of interception and seizure is properly videographed. The Commission
has also asked the election authorities to spread the message (Appeal) to public regarding Section 171
(B) [Bribery as Offence] and 171 (C) [Offence regarding threatening to candidate or elector] of IPC
during election period.

OFFICIAL LANGUAGE WING AND VIDHI SAHITYA PRAKASHAN
Recommendation/observation
1.0. The Committee express its concern over non utilisation of meager sums of ` 10.20 and ` 6.28 crore
funds year after year by Official Language Wing and Vidhi Sahitya Prakashan. The Committee
feels that the Department should proactively engage itself in these areas or it should realistically
project its requirements of funds. (Para 5.7)
Action Taken
1.1. Of ficial Languages Wing was allocated ` 8,92,00,000/- in R.E. 2015-16. Out of this,
` 8,82,05,000/- was utilized during the year 2015-16 and ` 9,94,144/- was left during the aforesaid
financial year. The unutilized amount of ` 9,94,144/- was in the salary head. Official Languages Wing
has been allocated an amount of ` 10.20 crore in BE-2016-17. Out of which ` 2.65 crore (26%) has
been utilized as on 31st July, 2016. The remaining amount will be utilized during the financial year
2016-17. This Wing has projected the budget for the financial year 2016-17 as per genuine requirement.
Vidhi Sahitya Prakashan has been allocated an amount of ` 6.28 crore in BE 2016-17 out of which
` 1.6 crore (25%) has been utilized as on 31st July, 2016 in the first quarter. During the year
2016-17 proposals are in consideration to fill up the vacant posts. Measures have been taken to purchase
required items/goods for office. Initiative has already been taken to pay the pending bills with the
Government Press for printing the Uchcha Nayayalaya Patrikas/Uchchatama Nayayalaya Patrikas. Proposal
of domestic travel under propagation of Hindi is under consideration.

Department of Legal Affairs
INCOME TAX APPELLATE TRIBUNAL (ITAT)
Recommendations/Observations
3.0. The Committee expresses its serious concerns over the declining rate of disposal of cases year after
year which has crossed more than one lakhs in 2014-15. The Institution of cases in ITAT has
progressively risen as compared to disposal from 2010-11. The Committee recommends ITAT to
take serious note of the rising pendency of cases and devise mechanism to reduce its pendency.
(Para 4.18)
Action Taken
3.1. The ITAT has taken the matter of rising pendency seriously, and adequate measures have been
taken to reduce the pendency. Consequently, during the financial year 2015-16, ITAT has disposed of
51010 appeals compared to 30494 appeals disposed of during the financial year 2014-15. This reveals
that ITAT has increased the disposal rate by 67.5 per cent over the previous financial year 2014-15.
Consequently, the total pendency has been reduced from 103238 to 91971, which is almost reduction
in total pendency by 11 per cent.
3.2. It may be mentioned that Section 255(3) of the Income Tax Act, 1961, has been amended by the
Finance Act, 2016, which authorizes the President or any Member of the Appellate Tribunal, sitting
singly, to dispose of any case which has been allotted to the Bench of which he is a member and which
pertains to an assessee whose total income as computed by Assessing Officer in the case does not
exceed Rs. 50 lakhs. Prior to said amendment, the ceiling of Single Member Bench was of Rs. 15 lakhs.
The enhancement of ceiling of Single Member Bench from ` 15 lakhs to ` 50 lakhs will help the tribunal
to reduce its pendency.
Further Observation
3.3. The Committee notes the reply and hopes that ITAT will ensure that pendency is brought
down significantly in the shortest possible time.
Recommendations/Observations
4.0. The Committee is also of the view that vacancies in the various Benches of the ITAT needs to
be filed up as non filling-up of this vacancies has direct bearing upon its disposal rate.
(Para 4.19)

13
Action Taken
4.1. The view of the Hon'ble committee that vacancies in the various Benches of ITAT has direct
bearing upon its disposal rate is correct. Continuous efforts are being made to fill up the post of Members
(Judicial/Accountant) of the ITAT. In this regard, it is submitted that during the financial year 2014-15,
ITAT had 68 Members against the sanctioned strength of 126. Since July, 2015, 42 new Members
(Judicial/Accountant) have been appointed in the ITAT. Out of these 42 Members, 2 Members have
resigned from the post. Appointment of these new members has paved the way for tribunal to dispose
of 51,010 Appeals during the financial year 2015-16 as compared to 30494 Appeals disposed of by the
Tribunal during the financial year 2014-15. This reveals that ITAT has increased the disposal rate by 67.5
per cent over the previous financial year 2014-15.
Further Observation
4.2. The Committee notes from the reply that more than 15 vacancies are yet to be filled and
there is still scope for increasing its disposal rate. The Committee feels that increase in the
monetary limit for disposal of cases by single member and filling of all vacancies shall help in
bringing down pendency and therefore department should make all out efforts to fill all vacancies
at the earliest.

Recommendations/Observations
5.0. NJA is an autonomous statutory institution being handled by Highest Judicial officers and sitting
Judges . The Committee desires that National Judicial Academy needs to establish regional academies
in East, South, West and Northern parts of the country to strengthen the training requirements of
judiciary at suitable locations, which may be other than State capitals. The Committee also feels

in the international legal system. The Committee also recommends the Government to encourage
the meeting of judges through reciprocal programmes by bi-lateral and multilateral arrangements
with all the countries and Regional Groupings. (Para 6.14)

GRAM NYAYALAYAS
Recommendations/Observations
6.0. The Committee expresses its concern at the slow pace of establishment of Gram Nyayalayas even
7 years after the enactment of the Act. Till date only 10 States have notified Gram Nyayalayas,
where highly populated States like Uttar Pradesh has only established 12 Gram Nyayalayas till
date. The Committee also feels that non-applicability of Gram Nyayalayas Act in Tribal Areas of
certain States is one of the reasons for its non-popularity. The Committee, accordingly, feels that
Gram Nyalayas be also extended to Tribal Areas so that these Gram Nyalayas become a link
between the regular justice system and Tribal justice system. (Para 6.50)
Action Taken
6.1. The Gram Nyayalaya Act, 2008 extends to the whole of India except to the States of Jammu and
Kashmir, Nagaland, Arunachal Pradesh, Sikkim and to the tribal areas specified in Parts I, II, IIA and
III of the Constitution of India within the States of Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura and Mizoram. In terms
of Section 3 (1) of the Gram Nyayalayas Act, 2008, it is for the State Governments to establish Gram
Nyayalayas in consultation with the respective High Courts. Majority of States have now set up regular
courts at Taluka level.
6.2. The issues relating to implementation of Gram Nyayalayas Scheme in the States were discussed
in the Conference of Chief Ministers of States and Chief Justices of High Courts on 7th April, 2013
wherein it was decided that the State Governments and High Courts should be left to decide the question
of establishment of Gram Nyayalayas, wherever feasible, taking into account their local problems. The
focus is, therefore, on setting up Gram Nyayalayas where regular courts have not been set up.
Further Observation
6.3. The Committee notes the reply. The Committee is further of the view that based on
experience so far gained the Department of Justice may examine the utility of Gram Nyalayas
in ensuring quick and cheap justice and easy access to justice and apprise the Committee of the
results thereof so that matter is considered further by the Committee.
USE OF REGIONAL LANGUAGES IN HIGH COURTS
Recommendations/Observations
7.0. The Committee reiterates its recommendations contained in Seventy-fifth Report on the Demands
for Grants (2015-16) wherein it observed that Article 348 provides for the use of Scheduled
languages, other than English, with the consent of the Governor of the State. The diversity of
languages spoken and enumerated in the Constitution of India clearly brings out the importance
of different languages of the country. The Committee, accordingly, feels that, scheduled languages
other than English may be permitted to be used in the High Courts, provided it is demanded by
the concerned State Government. The Committee is further of the view that the consultation

15
process with judiciary is not required as the Constitutional provisions are amply clear on the use
of Scheduled Languages in the High Courts and accordingly, the use of Scheduled Languages
should be decided as per mandate of Article 348. (Para 6.63)
Action Taken
7.1. The matters regarding implementation of the provisions of the Constitution relating to Official
language and the provisions of the Official Languages Act, 1963 (19 of 1963) except to the extent such
implementation has been assigned to any other Department and prior approval of the President for
authorising the limited use of a language other than English in the proceedings in the High Court of a
State have been assigned to the Department of Official Languages as per the Allocation of Business Rules,
1961.
7.2. The Secretary (Justice), vide DO letter dated 05.10.2015, had requested Secretary, Department of
Official Languages that the circumstances under which the 1965 decision of the Cabinet Committee were
taken and the circumstances obtaining today, alongwith the facility available for translation, etc., need
to be re-examined afresh. Hon'ble MLJ had also addressed Hon'ble Home Minister on 11.06.2015 to
consider review of the decision of the Cabinet (it might also be desirable to adopt a convention whereby
the Chief Justice of the India would be consulted on the proposals relating to use of Hindi and other
official languages of the States in the proceedings of the High Courts) taken 50 years ago.
7.3. The Department of Official Languages, in July, 2016, had forwarded a draft Cabinet Note suggesting
the following options before the Cabinet for decision: Either, the Cabinet convention adopted on 21.5.1965
is reconsidered and it is decided that the consultation of Chief Justice of India is not necessary before
the President gives his consent for use of Hindi/other Regional Languages in the proceedings of various
High Courts or the Cabinet convention adopted on 21.5.1965 regarding consultation with the Chief
Justice of India prior to President's consent is to be continued.
7.4. Department of Official Languages has mentioned that proposals for use of Bengali, Tamil, Gujarati,
Hindi and Kannada in the High Courts of Calcutta, Madras, Gujarat, Chhattisgarh and Karnataka, respectively,
under Article 348(2) of the Constitution, brought out by the respective State Governments, are pending
with them for conveying the prior consent of the President. However, all these proposals have been
disapproved by the Full Bench of the Supreme Court. It is also pertinent to mention that the issue of
use of Hindi/regional language(s) in the High Courts has often been raised by Hon'ble MPs within and
outside the Parliament.
Further Observation
7.5. The Committee notes the reply. The Committee, however, would like an early decision of
the cabinet on the options suggested by the Department of Official Languages and would like
to be informed of the decision taken by the Government in the matter.
Recommendations/Observations
8.0. As regards the Bombay, Madras & Calcutta High Courts, the Committee is of the view that the
names of these High Courts may be respectively changed to the new names, viz. 'High Court of

16
Maharashtra, Mumbai and Benches at Nagpur and Aurangabad; Tamil Nadu High Court at
Chennai and Bench at Madurai; and High Court of Kolkata, Bench at Andaman, Port Blair. This
will require a constitutional amendment. The Committee recommends the Department to move a
Bill in this regard so that names of these High Courts are accordingly changed. (Para 6.64)
Action Taken
8.1. The High Courts (Alteration of Names) Bill, 2016 enabling the changing the names of the High
Courts of Bombay, Calcutta and Madras into the High Courts of Mumbai, Kolkata and Chennai, respectively
has been introduced in the Lok Sabha on 19.07.2016. However, it is proposed to withdraw the Bill, as
the State Government of Tamil Nadu has requested to change the name of the 'High Court of Madras'
as the 'High Court of Tamil Nadu'.
Further Observation
8.2. The Committee notes the reply. The Committee hopes that its recommendations would be
given due consideration by the Department in the new Bill that may be drafted on withdrawal
of the pending Bill.

VACANCIES IN HIGHER JUDICIARY
Recommendations/Observations
2.0. The Committee is concerned with the large pendency of cases in Supreme Court and High Courts.
Approximately 45 per cent posts are vacant in High Courts as the Collegium system have failed to fill-
up vacancies in time. The Committee feels that without filling-up these vacancies, it will not be possible
for the High Courts to reduce its pendency as both are closely related. (Para 6.59)
Action Taken
2.1. As on 20.10.2016, out of an approved strength of 1079 in the High Courts, there is a working
strength of 620 Judges, leaving vacancies of 459 Judges. Vacancies have increased due to the following
reasons:
(a) No fresh appointments made during NJAC case from 13.04.2015 to 16.12.2015.
(b) Increase in strength of 173 Judges of various High Courts.
(c) Supreme Court Collegium rejects on average of 30% of recommendations.
17

18
2.2. Filling up of vacancies of Judges in the High Courts is a continuous and collaborative process of
the Judiciary and Executive. After the striking down the constitutional validity of the Constitution (Ninety-
Ninth Amendment) Act, 2014 and the National Judicial Appointments Commission Act, 2014, the Supreme
Court passed an order regarding improving the Collegium system in December, 2015 by supplementing
the existing Memorandum of Procedure (MoP). As the process was likely to take some time, at the
initiative of the Government, the matter was taken up with the Supreme Court and the process of
appointment of Judges has been resumed, pending finalization of the revised MoP. As a result, of the
concerted efforts 121 Additional Judges have been made permanent and 86 fresh appointments of Judges
have been made in various High Courts from 01.01.2016 to 05.10.2016. The shortage of Judges is not
the sole reason for inordinate delay in disposal of case. Cases are delayed on account of improper
investigation, lack of forensic laboratories, shortage of public prosecutors, recurrent adjournments and
improper application of rules and procedures. Further, it is also mentioned that Delhi and Gujarat have
a higher number of Judges per million of their respective population, they still have a high number of
pending cases.
Further Observation
2.3. The Committees is not at all satisfied with the reply of the Department. Department
cannot evade its responsibility in ensuring that vacancies in higher judiciary are filled up in the
shortest possible time by saying that other factors are also responsible for huge pendency in
higher courts. In its in Eighty-seventh Report on the "Inordinate Delay in Filling up the Vacancies
in the Supreme Court and High Courts" the Committee has examined the issue in depth and
given its recommendations. The Department should give effect to those recommendations of the
Committee and ensure that vacancies in higher judiciary are filled up as soon as these arise.
Recommendations/Observations
3.0. The Committee also reiterates its recommendations contained in its Thirty-ninth Report on Demands
for Grants (2010-11) and Eighty-Second Report on Action Taken Report on the recommendations/
observations contained in the 75th report on Demands for Grants (2015-16), that the retirement
age of judges of High Courts be increased to 65 years to bring it at par with the retirement age
of judges of Supreme Court of India by effecting amendment to the Constitution and related
legislation(s) and to help in easing the pressure of mounting vacancies in High Courts by passing
the Bill. (Para 6.60)
Action Taken
3.1. For increase the retirement age of High Court Judges from 62 to 65 the Constitution (One Hundred
and Fourteenth Amendment) Bill, 2010 was introduced in the Lok Sabha on 25.08.2010. The Bill was
referred to the Parliamentary Standing Committee for examination and report. The Committee in its
Forty-fourth Report on the Bill, recommended that the proposed Bill in its present form should be passed
without delay. However, the Bill could not be considered and lapsed due to dissolution of 15th Lok Sabha.
Further Observation
3.2. The Committee has recently examined the issue of retirement age of judges of higher
judiciary in its in Eighty-seventh Report of the Committee on the "Inordinate Delay in Filling

19
up the Vacancies in the Supreme Court and High Courts", wherein it has recommended that the
Government should increase the retirement age of the Supreme Court judge to 67 years and of
High Courts judge to 65 years.
Recommendations/Observations
4.0. The Committee feels that the Government should find avenues to generate revenue to meet
expenditure required for infrastructure requirements, supporting staff, etc. in the courts so as to make
them self - sustainable. The Committee accordingly, reiterates its recommendations contained in Seventy-
fifth Report on Demands for Grants (2015-16) that revenue should be raised from parties which can
afford to pay higher court fee, especially corporate houses for improving the basic amenities for Judges
and infrastructure. The surplus funds, if any, can also be utilised for improving the facilities of the
subordinate judiciary keeping in view that it is the sovereign duty of the Government to provide free
criminal justice. (Para 6.65)
Action Taken
4.1. A proposal was considered earlier for creation of a National Judicial Infrastructure Fund to be
managed by a Special Purpose Vehicle to carry out the work of infrastructure development of the
subordinate courts in the country. One of the proposed source of funding was enhanced court fees and
cost imposed on litigations. However, since the Planning Commission was of the view that creation of
the National Judicial Infrastructure Fund would be violation of Ministry of Finance guidelines on creation
of Reserve / Corpus funds, the proposal was dropped and was replaced by modified Centrally Sponsored
Scheme for development of infrastructure facilities for judiciary. A sum of Rs. 4,213 crore has been
released to the State Governments after revision of the Scheme in 2011 till 30th September, 2016.
Further Observation
4.2. The Committee is not satisfied with the reply of the Department. The Committee, therefore,
reiterates its recommendation contained in Seventy-fifth Report on Demands for Grants (2015-
16). The Committee is of the view that rich and corporate should be charged at premium rate
for civil and taxation cases so that surplus funds generated can be utilised for improving subordinate
judiciary, where majority of litigations relating to poor are pending.
Recommendations/Observations
5.0. The Committee feels that Government should make some efforts for raising the percentage of
women judges in the High Courts and the Supreme Court. The Committee insists that ideally the strength
of women judges should be around 50 percent of the total strength of the judges. [Para 6.66]
Action Taken
5.1. Appointment of Judges of the Supreme Court of India and High Courts are made under Articles
124, 217 and 224 of the Constitution of India, respectively, which do not provide for reservation for
any caste or class of persons.

20
5.2. However, keeping in view of diversity principle and giving due representation to various classes
of society in the appointment of Judges of the Supreme Court and High Courts, the Government has
been requesting the Chief Justices of the High Courts to take into consideration suitable candidates
belonging to Scheduled Castes, Scheduled Tribes, Minorities and Women while sending proposals for
appointment of Judges.
Further Observation
5.3. The Committee also examined the issue of representation of women and marginalised
sections in higher judiciary in its Eighty-seventh Report of the Committee on the "Inordinate
Delay in Filling up the Vacancies in the Supreme Court and High Courts". The Committee
reiterates the view taken in that Report that composition of higher judiciary should reflect the
diversity and composition of Indian society.
Department of Legal Affairs
INDIAN LA W INSTITUTE (ILI)
Recommendations/Observations
6.0. The Committee is constrained to note that the ILI has been dependent on the Government Grants-
in-aid. The Committee feels that ILI should generate its own fund by introducing relevant market driven
short-term courses as it cannot live forever by depending on Government grants. The Committee feels
that ILI needs to expand its activities and should explore moving into a bigger campus. The Committee
is of the view that it would be in fitness of things if ILI is given statutory backing. (Para 4.34)
Action taken
6.1. The ILI has reported that the Institute has leased out the first, second and third floor to Ministry
of Law & Justice. It is difficult for the Institute to introduce more academic course due to space
constraints and lack of infrastructure. The Institute has very less scope to earn more revenue through
expanded activities. The institute is in the process of exploring more avenues for expansion of its
activities both in terms of academic as well as infrastructure development by way of approaching
appropriate authority to allot land for a bigger campus. On the above observation of the Standing
Committee, ILI requested this Department to draft a legislation to place before the Parliament for
enactment of the Indian Law Institute as an Institute of National Repute like IITs, IIMs, and Central
University. Department of Legal Affairs is of the view that as the Institute has very less scope to
introduce more academic courses due to space constraints and lack of infrastructure, it may be appropriate
that ILI may first develop its infrastructure, and subsequently expand its academic activities. Thereafter,
matter relating to grant statutory backing to ILI may be considered by the Government at the appropriate
time.
Further Observation
6.2. In its recommendations, the Committee suggested for financial independence of ILI by
expanding its activities and thereby generating more revenues and also for the statutory back-

21
up to the institute. The reply by the Ministry does not comment on both the aspects rather gives
an evasive reply. The Committee fails to understand why this issue of the space constraint has
been highlighted particularly when the ILI has itself leased out its three floors to Ministry of
Law and Justice. The institute has, therefore, option to get these floors vacated and use the same
for expanded activities. Committee also does not agree with the Ministry's condition stipulating
that the statutory backing to ILI could be considered only after the requirement of space,
infrastructure, etc., are met. The Committee, therefore, impresses upon the Department of
Legal Affairs and the ILI to resolve the issues and take action as suggested by the Committee
in its said recommendation.

The Action Taken Report of the Committee deals with the action taken by the Ministry of Personnel,
Public Grievances and Pensions on the recommendations/observations of the Department-related
Parliamentary Standing Committee on Personnel, Public Grievances, Law and Justice in its Eighty-fifth
Report on the Demands for Grants (2016-17) of the Ministry. The Report was presented to Rajya Sabha
and laid on the Table of Lok Sabha on the 26th April, 2016.
2. The Action Taken Replies have been received from the Ministry of Personnel, Public Grievances
and Pensions in respect of the recommendations contained in the above mentioned Report, vide, their
communications dated on 30th May, 2016, 31st August, 2016 and 23rd September, 2016. These replies
have been categorised as follows :
CHAPTER-I: The recommendations/observations which have been accepted by the Ministry
i.e., in respect of paras 27, 30.7.2, 30.7.3, 31.3, 32.4, 32.5, 33.3, 34.3, 37.3,
38.4, 41.3, 41.5, 42.4, 42.6, 42.7, 43.3 and 43.4 of the Report. The Committee
is pleased to note that the Ministry has accepted these recommendations.
CHAPTER-II: The recommendations/observations which the Committee does not desire to pursue
in view of the replies given by the Ministry i.e., in respect of paras 31.2, 35.3,
35.4, 36.3, 36.4 and 42.5 of the Report. The Committee is satisfied with the
explanations advanced by the Ministry and does not wish to pursue them as of
now.
CHAPTER-III: The recommendations/observations in respect of which Committee is not satisfied
with the replies given by the Ministry i.e., with regard to paras 30.3, 30.7.1, 28,
29, 33.4, 34.4 and 40.2 of the Report. The Committee does not accept the reasons
given for not accepting the recommendations of the Committee and reiterates its
recommendations.

5.1. Lokpal and Lokayuktas Act, 2013 requires some amendments so as to provide for situations where

4

when the need for vigilance clearance arises, has been noted by DoPT and the same is under examination.

from CAT for creation of post or promotion or any other issue, the same is taken care of and disposed
of appropriately. As regards to recommendations related to functioning of CAT as mediator between
employees and Government, the same has been communicated to CAT for necessary action.
Further Observation
7.4. The Committee takes note of the reply.
UNION PUBLIC SERVICE COMMISSION (UPSC)
Measures for reduction of time taken in recruitment process
Recommendation/observation
8.0. The Committee appreciates that the UPSC has devised ways to shorten the duration of time taken
from the time of publication of advertisement to time of actual recruitment and also with regard to DPCs

6
for promotions and deputations. However, it is constrained to point out that the earlier recommendations
of the Committee to explore the feasibility of adopting a computerized GMAT kind of system having
validity of the score for at least three years in the preliminary stage of examinations has not so far been
made applicable by the UPSC. The Committee therefore reiterates is earlier recommendation to explore
a modality akin to the GMAT system in order to save on the expenditure on stationery as well as
processing time of the examinations at the earliest time possible. (Para 34.3)

8.1. The Commission continues efforts to further shorten the time taken from the publication of the
advertisement to the time of actual recruitment. It may be mentioned that the CSE is being comprehensively
reviewed by a Committee of Experts and the terms of reference includes an examination of use of ICT
in the CSE.
Further Observation
8.2. The Committee takes note of the reply.
FIXED TENURE OF IAS, IPS & IFS
Recommendation/observation
9.0. In this context the Committee views that the DoPT should impress upon the State Governments
to strictly comply with the service rules relating to tenure of the high ranking officers in service so that
the officers are able to discharge their duty without fear. (Para 37.3)
Action Taken
9.1. It is stated that in the matter of Shri. T.S.R Subramanian, the Hon'ble Supreme Court directed the
Central Government and all the State Governments for setting up of Civil Services Board for IAS, IPS
and IFS and to provide minimum tenure to All India Service officers. The relevant amendments in Rule
7 were carried out and the notification dated 28.01.2014 (Annexure-I) was issued by this Department
in compliance of Apex Court's judgment.
9.2 Further amendments were proposed by State Government of Uttar Pradesh in Rule 7 of IAS
(Cadre) Rules, 1954 and same was discussed in the GAD meeting of all State/UT Government on
08.09.2015. All the State Governments agreed to the amendments as proposed by the State Government
of Uttar Pradesh. The Proposed amendments in Rule 7 of the IAS (Cadre) Rules, 1954 were notified
on 13.04.2016 (Annexure-II) by the Services Division.
Further Observation
9.3. The Committee takes note of the reply.
RECRUITMENT DRIVE FOR PERSONS WITH DISABILITIES (PWD)
Recommendation/observation
10.0. The Committee desires that posts reserved for PWDs which could not be filled up should be carried
forward and not transferred to another category. The Department should take all out effort to fill up

7
vacancies under reserved categories and not take the plea of not finding any candidate eligible. The
Committee further recommends that the eligibility criteria for these reserved posts be reviewed, where
eligible candidates are scarce and skill development approach should be applied to absorb them into the
system. (Para 38.4)
Action Taken
10.1. Section 32 of the Persons with Disabilities (Equal Opportunities, Protection of Rights and Full
Participation) Act, 1995 (PWD Act) provides for identification of posts which can be reserved for
Persons with Disabilities.
10.2. The Department of Empowerment of Persons with Disabilities administers the PWD Act.
10.3. Department of Empowerment of Persons with Disabilities identify posts suitable for each category
viz. (i) blindness or low vision (ii) hearing impairment and (iii) locomotor disability or cerebral palsy, in
the posts identified for each disability.
10.4. Though there is a provision in the Section 36 of the PWD for carrying forward of vacancies for
Persons with Disability and subsequent interchange of vacancies among the three categories in case of
non-availability of candidates, the Government has taken steps to fill up vacancies identified for respective
category of person with disability through instruction issued in May, 2015 to carry out Special Recruitment
Drive.
10.5. Thirteen Inter-Ministerial Committee Meetings at the level of Secretary (Personnel) have been held
between June, 2015 to May, 2016 to monitor the filling up of vacancies for Persons with Disabilities.
12377 vacancies for the persons with disabilities have been filled up. Concerted and continuous efforts
are being made to fill up vacancies identified for each category of person with disability.
10.6. A Committee under the Chairmanship of Secretary, Department of Social Justice and Empowerment
was constituted in July, 2013 comprising representatives from 20 Ministries/Departments to make in-
depth analysis of the reasons for non-filling up reserved vacancies/less employability of SCs, STs, OBCs
and Persons with Disabilities (PWDs) in Government sector and to suggest remedial measures. Keeping
in view the recommendations of the Committee, time bound deliverables have been identified and intimated
to Ministries/Departments to constitute in-house Expert Committee, preparation of data-sheet in regard
to backlog vacancies, study the reasons for non-filling up of reserved posts, identify more posts for
persons with disabilities and to fill up such vacancies, including those of persons with disabilities.
Further Observation
10.7. The Committee takes note of the reply.
DEPARTMENT OF ADMINISTRATIVE REFORMS & PUBLIC GRIEVANCES
Pilot Projects on Administrative Reforms
Recommendation/observation
11.0. "While taking note of the steps taken by the Department of Administrative Reforms with regard
to modernization of Government Offices, the Committee is of the view that the Department should not

8
merely play the role of a funding agency for the schemes, but should take upon itself the task of
monitoring the effective execution of the schemes in the offices undergoing modernization.
11.1. While the Committee appreciate advocacy of Good Governance and Best Practices in public
administration through informative booklets, pamphlets, CDs etc. by the Department, it advocate that
implementation of these schemes should not only confine to printing of information material but actual
achievements of principles and targets envisaged in the scheme and policies, should be accomplished
through other innovative means and continuous training and skill development." (Para 41.3)
Action Taken
11.2. After the release of funds, the Additional Secretary, DARPG regularly reviews the implementation
of modernization of projects and utilization of funds. At the end of financial year, this review is done
almost on a daily basis. The concerned officials of the Department also visit the site of the projects.
11.3. The objective of PM Award Scheme is to acknowledge, recognise and reward the extraordinary
and innovative work done by officials/ organizations of the Central, State Governments, Autonomous
Bodies, Urban Local Bodies, Panchayats, ZilaParishads. To meet this objective and also to take advantage
of benefits accrue to the best practices, the Department is making following efforts:
(i) Pursuing State/UTs to replicate the PM Award winning initiatives in their States/UTs according
to their suitability. In this connection number of meetings with State/UT Govt. have been
held through video conferencing. With the result out of 17 initiatives awarded PM Award
on 21st April, 2015, 23 States and one UT have identified 14 initiatives for replication in
their States/UTs as per their suitability. As this is a huge task which needs to be completed
in a time bound manner, the Department has also engaged Administrative Staff College of
India (ASCI), Hyderabad to give technical support in this project. The ASCI has been
mandated to visit different sites (approx.100) across the country and also to conduct
workshop, meeting etc. with State and Central Governments so that best practices identified
by the States could be rolled out in an effective and time bound manner and benefit out of
these initiatives could reach to the common citizen in a shortest possible time.
(ii) The Department operates a scheme under State Collaboration Initiative (SCI) for funding
to the States/UT Governments for improvement in public administration and public service
delivery system. The Department has revised the guidelines to include funding to the project
of the State/UT Govt. for replicating PM Awarded initiatives.
(iii) The Department imparts foreign training to the Champions of Award winning initiatives.
(iv) The Department carries out Research & Evaluation study of the PM Awarded initiatives.
The study report then circulated to the all State/ Central Training Institutes for training
purpose.
Further Observation
11.4. The Committee takes note of the reply.

9
Recommendation/Observation
12.0. The Committee appreciates the initiative of the Department in involving International Experts to
analyse and study the e-governance methods, processes and technology employed by Government institutions
which will be indicative of the country's actual standing in the international standards. The move for
a Knowledge Repository is also welcome. It hopes the endeavour of the Department to take the country
at par with the e-Governance practices of other advanced countries will be realized very soon.
(Para 41.5)
Action Taken
12.1. UNDP has been partnering with DARPG since the last quarter of 2013. The key focus of the
project is to assist in the area of administrative reforms and Government Business process Re-engineering
through e-governance and sharing of knowledge on global best practices. Last year in August, 2015, the
focus of the partnership took a new turn with the Department shifting its focus to improving India's
e-governance through online citizen-centric services and thereby, improving India's global ranking in the
UN e-Government Development Index 2018. DARPG has asked UNDP's assistance in bringing out a
comprehensive e-Governance Roadmap with short-term actions primarily focused on these milestones
that would help in enhancing India's global ranking. Some of the short- term actions have been completed
in 2015, other need to be completed along with the medium-term actions by mid-July, 2016. Actions are
to be taken on the following activities as per Annual Work Plan 2016.
(a) Bring out a sub-National e-Government Index with targets to motivate States in enhancing
their online citizen-centric services delivery.
(b) Consolidate e-Governance services through the India National Portal and standardize channel
interfaces.
Further Observation
12.2. The Committee takes note of the reply.
PUBLIC GRIEV ANCE REDRESSAL
Recommendation/Observation
13.0. The Committee takes note of the colossal increase in the number of grievances received lately and
the corresponding disposal of the Grievances by the concerned Departments. It is of the conviction that
the essence of good governance is defeated in the absence of efficient and timely redressal of grievance.
Therefore, the DARPG should keep close vigil over monitoring of grievance redressal in every Ministry/
Department. (Para 42.4)
Action Taken
13.1. Monitoring of pendency of Grievances is being done regularly through review meetings held
monthly. 22 such review meetings have been held during 2014-2015 which have been attended by almost
all the Ministries/Departments.

10
Further Observation
13.2. The Committee takes note of the reply. The Ministry should, however, take measures to
ensure that the rate of disposal of grievances is increased and quality disposal of grievances is
made.
Recommendation/Observation
14.0. "Good Governance" is reflected by the peoples' satisfaction on the working of, accessibility to,
delivery of services by the system whereas a large number of grievance petitions show a Department in
a bad light. The Committee is of the view that the spirit of Public Grievances Redressal Mechanism is
primarily to resolve the grievances to the satisfaction of the petitioner. The Committee strongly feels that
the relief and remedial mechanism should also fix the accountability on the decision making authorities.
The Committee notes that the data provided to the Committee does not reflect the satisfaction of the
petitioners in respect of the redressal of their grievances. The Committee is apprehensive that in the event
of dissatisfaction of petitioners on the redressal of their grievances, the petitioners are bound to approach
courts for redressal of their grievances. Hence, the Committee desires that the Department of Administrative
Reforms and Public Grievances should conduct a study to find out the number of complainants who had
gone to courts/tribunals and how many cases the courts/tribunals ruled in favour of the petitioners. It
further desires that while submitting the ATRs, the findings of the study may be furnished for the
consideration of the Committee. (Para 42.6)
Action Taken
14.1. The Department of Administrative Reforms and Public Grievances has no such information regarding
complainants who have approached courts/tribunals on being dissatisfied with the grievance redressal and
have got favourable recourse from the courts. Information regarding Court Cases arising out of non-redress
of public grievance is being collected. A study is also being proposed to be undertaken on this issue after
which the findings will be furnished to the Committee.
Further Observation
14.2. The Committee takes note of the reply. The Department should, however, furnish the
information once it is collected by it as also the results of proposed study to the Committee.
ROLE OF DARPG
Recommendation/Observation
15.0. The DARPG should realize the crucial role of the Department in this regard and having so many
high cadre officers should take a pro active stand to see that these recommendations are implemented
in war footing mode to give "Good Governance" in real time basis. (Para 42.7)
Action Taken
15.1. The Department has noted the observations of the Committee.

11
Further Observation
15.2. The Committee takes note of the reply.
Department of Pension & Pensioners' Welfare
CENTRALIZED PENSION GRIEV ANCE REDRESS AND MONITORING SYSTEM (CPENGRAMS)
Recommendation/Observation
16.0. The Committee desires that this Department should play a role as an apex level coordination entity
for addressing the grievances of pensioners. The Committee is of the firm belief that pension is a right
and not merely a privilege. It welcomes the initiatives 'Bhavishya', 'Sankalp' and 'Anubhav' and hopes
that maximum pensioners will be benefited by these initiatives. The Committee, at the same time is very
much concerned about their welfare and accordingly recommends that nodal officers should be appointed
in every Department including PSUs in their respective establishments to attend to the welfare of
pensioners and represent them if required to the concerned authorities. (Para 43.3)
Action Taken
16.1. Implementation of pension policy is dealt with in respective Ministries/Departments and their
subordinate formations, from where the employee retires as well as the pension disbursing authority.
Nodal Officers for pension related grievances have been nominated in all Ministries/ Departments. Details
are available on the Pensioners' Portal website. Since the matters relating to welfare of pensioners (except
policy issues) are to be dealt with by respective Ministries/ Departments, the recommendations of the
Standing Committee as made in para 43.3 have been communicated to all Ministries/ Departments
including those regarding appointment of Nodal Officers for pensioners welfare in every PSU and will
be followed up.
Further Observation
16.2. The Committee takes note of the reply.
Recommendation/Observation
17.0. The Committee feels that every public servant will eventually become a pensioner in their lifetime.
The Trade Union and Employees/Officers Union of Organisations/Departments may be allowed to negotiate
with their employer for improvement of the post-retirement issues along with the existing service conditions.
The Government can also use the expertise of the post retiree citizens productively in various fields in
order to boost their morale and give them renewed zest to life. The Government should also approach
the elder citizens (retirees) in positive way by calling annual meetings and discuss their welfare. Therefore,
the Committee recommends that the Department should give serious consideration to these suggestions.
(Para 43.4)
Action Taken
17.1. W ith a view to use the expertise of pensioners productively the Department has launched a web
enabled application - Sankalp which aims at channelizing skill, experience and time available with retired

12
government servants into meaningful, voluntary contribution to society. This would add to the social
capital of the country and at the same time restore dignity and purpose to life post-retirement.
17.2 The Department, on the recommendation of Parliamentary Consultative Committee, has also
constituted a Standing Committee of Voluntary Agencies (SCOVA) to mobilize the voluntary efforts to
supplement the Government action. It is a useful forum for holding consultation with the pensioners
through their Associations and provides them an opportunity for raising their problem directly before the
concerned Ministries, as the official of these Ministries are also present in the meeting. The meetings
of SCOV A also provide valuable feedback to the Government for effective implementation of the programmes
and give direction for the future course of action. Due representation has been given to various Pensioners'
Associations in the SCOVA. The meeting of SCOV A is held twice a year and are chaired by Hon'ble MOS
(PP).
17.3 The recommendation of the Standing Committee, as made out in para 43.4 of their subject Report,
have been brought to the notice of all Ministries/ Departments for further appropriate action.
Further Observation
17.4. The Committee takes note of the reply.

CHAPTER-II
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS WHICH THE COMMITTEE DOES NOT DESIRE TO
PURSUE IN VIEW OF THE REPLIES GIVEN BY THE MINISTRY
Department of Personnel & Training
LAL BAHADUR SHASTRI NATIONAL ACADEMY OF ADMINISTRATION (LBSNAA)
Shortage of trainers at LBSNAA
Recommendation/observation
1.0. The Committee expects that the premier training institution of the country ought to be adequately
equipped not only in physical terms but also in terms of its manpower. Due to the fact that the whole
system of governance is now changing and the international pressure and expectations are now high,
flexibility has to be brought into the system. In that context, all training programmes confined to one
location may not be the single answer to the existing problem of shortage of manpower. Accordingly,
other feasible options of handling the situation may be explored. At the same time, the DoPT should
evolve a policy which can address this constraint of the LBSNAA. (Para 31.2)
Action Taken
1.1. Academy is utilizing the services of other training academies/Institutes by conducting special /
parallel foundation and induction training courses.
Further Observation
1.2. The Committee takes note of the reply. However, DoPT should evolve a policy to address
the acute shortage of trainers.
STAFF SELECTION COMMISSION (SSC)
Computer based examination
Recommendation/Observation
2.0. The Committee appreciates the initiatives of the SSC in adopting the Computer based mode of
conducting its examinations which has reduced the time taken from filling up of applications by the
candidates to declaration of results. The Committee hopes that more efforts for better management may
be invested by both the Commission which would further reduce the time. It is of the firm belief that
the time of the young applicants is very valuable and therefore, the Commission should make all out
efforts to not waste their time by making long lapses in declaring result of examinations.  (Para 35.3)
2.1 In view of the high increase in number of applicants, the Committee recommends that commensurate
enhancement in the budgetary allocation should also be made by the DoPT. As the SSC adopted the
13

14
Computer base mode of conducting examinations, the Committee desires that all caution should be taken
to ensure that examinations are inaccessible to candidates from far flung and rural areas were commodities
such as electricity, computers are scarce. The Committee further recommends that the SSC should ensure
to authenticate institutions in rural areas to train the youths in those rural areas with regard to the
computer system. (Para 35.4)
Action Taken
2.2. The Staff Selection Commission (SSC) is mandated to conduct eight All India Open Competitive
Examinations in a year. The Commission has been conducting these examinations in the OMR Based
Mode and in the current year the Commission has been requested to conduct Combined Graduate Level
Examination, 2016 in the Computer Based Mode. The Commission has already conducted the Re-
examination of Sub-Inspectors in Delhi Police, Central Armed Police Forces (CAPFs) and Assistant Sub-
Inspectors in CISF Examination 2016 in the Computer Based Mode in June 2016. The decision to change
the mode of conduct of examination from OMR Based Mode to Computer Based Mode is expected to
increase confidentiality in Question Paper Management and Administration, faster processing of results
by the SSC besides better data management.
2.3 The Government has requested the Commission to conduct the Combined Graduate Level
Examination, 2016, i.e. the flagship examination of the Commission in Computer Based Examination
Mode. The Government has also requested the SSC to take expeditious steps to revamp the scheme of
other examinations conducted by it on the lines of the changes approved for CGLE.
2.4 The Commission has exercised due caution and taken initial measures to ensure that the computer
based examinations are easily accessible to candidates from far flung and rural areas. These measures
inter-alia include:
(i) Simplification of the format / procedures for on-line registration for candidates from far
flung and rural areas;
(ii) Uploaded an 'animated walk through module' on the website of the Commission and its
Regional Offices, to comprehensively educate the candidates on the salient processes entailed
for conduct of the computer based examinations.
2.5. Uploaded practice tests' and mock drills' for candidates on the website of the Commission and its
Regional Offices so that candidates can regularly practice and adapt themselves to the computer based
mode of examinations.
Further Observation
2.6. The Committee takes note of the reply. The Committee also appreciates the conducting
of Computer based examinations by the SSC in the year 2016 and the steps taken for making
such examinations accessible to candidates from far flung and rural areas.
CENTRAL INFORMATION COMMISSION (CIC)
Pendency of cases in CIC
Recommendation/Observation
3.0. The Committee takes note of the upcoming building for the CIC which on completion, it hopes,
will boost the morale of the CIC and in turn will result in the greater efficiency of the Commission. With

15
regard to the pendency of cases with the Commission, the Committee recommends that the CIC should
take holistic approach to ensure that the cases pending with it are disposed off in a time-bound manner.
(Para 36.3)

3.1. As per MoU signed between CIC and NBCC, the date of Completion (likely) of the new CIC
building under construction is 31.03.2018.
With regard to pendency of cases with the Commission, recently Central Govt. has appointed three
more Information Commissioners in the Commission bringing the Commission to work in its full strength
for the first time, i.e. 1 CIC and 10 ICs. This would help the Commission to expedite the disposal of
pending cases. Further, with the strengthening of e-governance in the Commission, the process of
disposal of Appeals/Complaints will be expedited.
Further Observation
3.2. The Committee takes note of the reply, and hopes that with the Commission working with
its full strength, pace of disposal of cases would significantly improve and pendency of cases
reduce.
SUO MOTU DISCLOSURE BY PUBLIC AUTHORITIES UNDER RTI
Recommendation/Observation
4.0. In this context, the Committee is of the view that the purpose of the institution of RTI and thereby
the CIC is to ensure transparency in the working of the Government and not to institute another platform
of justice dispensation. Therefore, the CIC should function more as a mediator between the information
seeker and the information giver. On the other hand, all department and ministries should be encouraged
for voluntary disclosure of information as per Section 2(4) of the RTI Act. All information providers,

to inform how the tax-payers money is spent. (Para 36.4)

4.1. W ith a view to maximize suo-motu disclosure by public authorities so that citizens need not resort
to filling RTI applications to obtain information, guidelines had been issued to all the Ministries/Departments
of Govt. of India on 15.04.2013. DoPT has further issued instructions to all Public Authorities vide O.M.
No. 1/1/2013-IR, dated 9th July, 2015(Annexure-III)that the Departments must take an analysis of
information which is sought most often from applicants and provide it on their website as suo-motu
disclosure.
4.2. Another OM No. 1/34/2013-IR dated 30th June, 2016 (Annexure-IV) has been issued giving
directions to all Public Authorities under Central Government to inter alia improve their mechanisms of
suo-motu disclosure through:
(i) Constitution of Consultative Committees of stakeholders,
(ii) Having Information and Facilitation Centers,

16
(iii) Proper categorization and organization of information that is disclosed for its easy
retrieval, and
(iv) To undertake Transparency audit of their suo-motu disclosure.
4.3. Further, CIC is taking necessary measures for improvement in the quality of suo-motu disclosure
under Section 4(1)b.
Further Observation
4.4. The Committee takes note of the reply and further recommends that the CIC may also
insure that its instructions in this regard are adhered to by the Public Authorities.

Public Grievance Redressal
Recommendation/observation
5.0. The Committee welcomes the initiative taken by the Department to assess and analyse the quality
of grievance redressal in the Ministries/Departments of the Government of India. It hopes that the
Department will continue the exercise with other Ministries/Departments as well. The Committee further

Further Observation
5.2. The Committee takes note of the reply and appreciates the efforts of the Department for
not only disposing of Grievances but assessing and analyzing the quality of grievance redressal
in the Ministries/Departments of the Government of India. The data thus collected from various
Ministries/Department should be uploaded on the website of the Department.

CHAPTER-III
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS IN RESPECT OF WHICH COMMITTEE HAS NOT
ACCEPTED REPLIES OF THE MINISTRY
DEPARTMENT OF PERSONNEL & TRAINING
Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI)
Reduction of Budgetary allocation
Recommendation/Observation
1.0. The Committee strongly recommends for making adequate funds available to the CBI to enable
it to implement its Plan schemes to the ideal stipulation. The Committee is however unable to understand
why the allocation of ` 85.07 BE (2015-16) was reduced to ` 75.25 crore at the RE stage and then to
` 75.00 crore as BE this year. The Committee however surmises that fund reductions could be for the
reason that the spending units, CBI in this case, were unable to utilise 50% of the funds within the first
six months of the financial year, hence funds got reduced at next year's BE. The Committee apprehends
that such a reduction may affect the pace of implementation of schemes. The Ministry in their action
taken replies should clarify the same, explain the reasons for such reductions and also suggest how it
can be avoided. Meanwhile, the Committee recommends to the CBI to beef up the pace of the
implementation of its proposed schemes. (Para 30.3)
Action Taken
1.1. Funds as demanded by CBI in BE-2016-17 has been provided to them. At present, CBI has made
'Nil' requirement of funds in first batch of demand for Supplementary. As far as under utilization of 50%
of the funds within the first six months of the financial year 2015-16 is concerned, CBI has stated the
reasons and action taken in the current year as tabulated in Annexure-V .
Further Observation
1.2. The Committee expresses its serious concern over non utilization of funds owing to procedural
reasons which could have been avoided with better monitoring. Considering the responsibility
entrusted to the CBI these procedural hassles needs to be addressed so that funds made available
to the agency are utilized and the schemes are implemented as per schedule. The Committee
accordingly impress upon the DoPT & the CBI to take necessary measures so that under-
utilizations of funds is avoided in future.
VACANCY POSITION IN CBI
Recommendation/Observation
2.0. The Committee expresses deep concern on the state of affairs relating to the vacancy position in
the CBI. It therefore impresses upon the DoPT to complete the exercise of cadre review by June, 30, 2016
17

18
as per the direction of the Supreme Court to deal with the vacancy position of the establishment. The
Committee is apprehensive that unless the present malady of massive vacancy is not corrected immediately,
the very purpose of establishment of the CBI would be eroded and its credibility tarnished. At this
juncture when the nation envisages the premier investigating agency of the country to be at par with their
international counterparts, performance and result oriented and equipped to combat the challenges of
international pressures of transnational terrorism, cyber-crimes and corruption, the Committee is disheartened
that the CBI is crippled with a very basic requirement, shortage of manpower.
Action Taken
2.1. The Central Bureau of Investigation, as a multi disciplinary premier investigation agency, investigates
cases wherein sensitivity and dimensions require high degree of expertise, hard work, professionalism
and responsibility. Due to the deputationist character of the Bureau, there will always be certain vacancies
due to the cyclical nature of officers coming and going on deputation, and active cases seeking new
officers on deputation are always under process. The number of vacancies keeps on varying depending
on the induction, promotion, repatriation and retirement of officers. Department of Personnel & Training
concerned with filling up posts of level of SP and above in CBI has filled up a number of vacant posts
at senior level on the recommendations of CBI Selection Committee headed by CVC. CBI, responsible
with filling up vacancies at junior level executive posts, has made persistent efforts to fill up these posts
by various methods of recruitment. DoPT as well as CBI has pursued with UPSC to expedite recruitment
process in respect of various vacant executive / legal / technical posts in CBI at different levels. CBI
has also taken steps for conducting DPCs to expedite appointments for vacant executive posts at various
levels by promotion in time bound manner. Further, CBI is in the process of reviewing its Recruitment
Rules and an Internal Committee has been constituted for this purpose to expedite the recruitment
process. The recruitments made during 2015-16 & 2016-17 are furnished in Annexure-VI.
Further Observation
2.2. The Committee is of the view that the CBI must ensure adequate staffing in order to deal
with the rising burden of investigations. The process for recruitment of manpower on deputation
should be initiated well in advance before the vacancies arise, so that the gap between occurrence
of vacancies and their filling is reduced to the minimum possible. The Committee is however
constrained to note that the information given in ATR does not categorically explain the actual
status of vacancies. The Committee desires to be apprised with the actual status of vacancies.
The Committee accordingly advises that proactive steps must be undertaken to fill up the
existing vacancies in a time bound manner .
IMPLEMENTATION OF 24 REPORT OF THE COMMITTEE ON CBI
Recommendation/Observation
3.0 With cases being referred by States and Courts to the CBI for investigation, the Committee
acknowledges the burden of load bestowed upon it. However, it is of the concerted views that, the CBI
turn to the State or other Central Forces to plug the vacancy in the establishment. It therefore, desires
that the CBI manage its cadre more efficiently and the DoPT should take holistic steps to hasten the
part of recruitment in consultation with the UPSC. For that matter, the Committee strongly recommends

19
the DoPT to revisit the 24th Report of the Committee on 'The Working of the Central Bureau of
Investigation (CBI)' wherein, after an exhaustive examination and intensive study of the issues, had
recommended workable ways to strengthen the CBI which included an enactment for the CBI.
(Para 30.7.1)
Action Taken
3.1. The 24th Report of the Committee on 'The Working of the Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI)'
had given recommendations for strengthening CBI. The most of the recommendations have so far been
implemented by the Government. The major decisions taken from time to time to strengthen CBI are:-
(a) Director CBI has been delegated financial powers equivalent to Director Generals of CAPFs
and CRPF vide DoPT's orders dated 22.07.2013 and 22.01.2014.
(b) The amendments to the Delhi Special Police Establishment (DSPE) Act, 1946 have been
made through the Lokpal and Lokayuktas Act, 2013, providing for appointment of the
Director, CBI and the Director of Prosecution, CBI in order to give them autonomy and
independence.
(c) Director CBI has further been given more administrative powers to strengthen CBI like
recruitment to the post of DySP in exemption from consultation of UPSC for recruitment
to the post of Dy SP for a period of three year, extension in the deputation tenure of
Inspectors in CBI upto 10th year, seeking first stage advice in disciplinary cases against CBI
officers directly from CVC, etc.
(d) To further strengthen CBI, 598 posts have been created in CBI during the year 2015-16.
To make it a modern and efficient organization, Government has taken various measures
which inter alia include modernization, improvement in training, infrastructure, housing and
improving condition of work and employment of staff of the CBI. A Plan outlay of Rs 309
crores under various schemes in the 12th plan have been provided for CBI.
(e) Furthermore, two separate schemes for establishment of Centralized Technology Vertical
(CTV)-CBI and International Center for Excellence in Investigation (ICEI)-CBI are under
consideration in the Department.
(f) CBI, since submission of 24th Report of the Committee on 'The Working of the Central
Bureau of Investigation (CBI)', has grown into more dynamic and efficient organization with
aforesaid measures strengthening CBI. The subject of bringing a separate statute for CBI
has been considered and it has been concluded that the Constitution would require to be
amended, which may also impinge on the federal structure of the Constitution and the
mandate of Parliament to enact a law which would be in conflict with Entry 2 of List II
which is in the domain of the States. Therefore, it is not open to the Central Government
to constitute a CBI and confer on it powers which will impinge on all the powers of
investigation of offences which are conferred on the state police.
Further Observation
3.2. The Committee is of the view that the powers given to the CBI under DSPE Act are not
adequate enough considering the pace of changing times and in this context the Committee
recommended for a separate statute for CBI. Further, the apprehensions raised by the Department

20
have been adequately answered in its Twenty-fourth report of the Committee. Thus the Committee
reiterates its recommendations made in this regard.

Recommendation/Observation
4.0. The AS & FA of the Ministry had given justifications for the reduction of the funds allocated for
LBSNAA that the Academy did not make a fifty per cent utilization by September of the financial year

the spending unit has not assessed its targets thoroughly before making the projections. It, therefore,

as on that date when furnishing the Action Taken Replies of this Report. (Para 28)

levels and all Organisations/Divisions are suitably instructed to ensure to assess their targets thoroughly

Grant No.64 is attached at  Annexure-VII.

4.3. The Committee notes that as per the Statement of Expenditure as on 31st August, 2016,
the LBSNAA has been able to utilize only 22.90% of plan expenditure and 17.68% of non-plan

allotted funds are strictly adhered to by these organizations.

early commencement of its schemes/projects to ensure the 50% utilization of the funds before September

Spending Unit is monitored on a regular basis at senior levels and all concerned Divisions / Organisations

September, 2016.

5.3. The Committee takes note that as per the Statement of Expenditure as on 31st August,

of their plan and non-plan expenditure which is not in tandem with the M/o Finance instructions
of utilization of 50% of allotted budget by September of the current financial year. This means
either units are projecting fund requirements which are more than actuals or implementation/
expenditure is non efficient and both these situations reflect poorly on the Department. The
Department should ensure that projection of funds by units is realistic and monitoring is effective
enough to ensure proper utilization of funds.

Grievance Redressal Mechanism

6.0. The Committee is of the concerted opinion that employees frustrated with the service condition
approach Courts, including CAT where they end up waiting for years for the judgment and thereby the
entire system is adversely affected. The Committee feels that many of the cases in service matters can
be settled by mediation within the system itself. The Committee is of the opinion that in the administration,
the senior officer be made duty-bound to resolve the grievances of the subordinate officers. He is
expected to sit along with the aggrieved and decide the matter, get the concurrence of the supreme
authority and complete the entire process. The tribunals/ Courts are needed to be resorted to, only in
the rarest matters. Thus, the Committee calls for a drastic change in the attitude of the administration.

6.1. Redressal of grievances system is already there where a Government employee can approach to
higher officers for redressal of his grievance. Also as per CAT Act, a Tribunal shall not ordinarily admit

relevant service rules as to redressal of grievances.

6.2. The in-house Grievance Redressal system in the organization should effectively deal with
the grievances of the employees. The Committee has, therefore, suggested that a nodal officer
of senior level be appointed to ensure redressal of grievances. If grievances are satisfactorily

reiterates its recommendation in this regard and Govt. should take steps to enhance the efficacy

INTRODUCTION 
 I, the Chairman of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Personnel, Public 
Grievances, Law and Justice, having been authorised by the Committee, present its Ninth Report relating to the 
Arbitration and Conciliation (Amendment) Bill*, 2003. The Bill seeks to amend the Arbitration and 
Conciliation Act, 1996. 
2. In pursuance of the rules relating to the Department Related Parliamentary Standing Committee, the 
Hon’ble Chairman, Rajya Sabha referred** the Bill, as in troduced in the Rajya Sabh a on the 22nd December, 
2003 and pending therein, to the Committee, for examination and report. Earlier when this Committee was not 
in existence, the Bill was referred to the Department Related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Home 
Affairs on the 8th January, 2004. Consequent upon the dissolution of the 13th Lok Sabha on the 6th February, 
2004, the Committee was dissolved. The present Committ ee came into existence after bifurcation of the 
Department Related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Home Affairs on 20th July, 2004. 
3.  Keeping in view the importance of the Bill, the Committee in its meeting held on the 23rd August 2004, 
decided to issue Press Communique to solicit views/suggestions from interested 
individuals/organisations/institutions on various provisions of the Bill. 
4.  In response to the Press Communique, 59 memora nda containing the suggestions were received by the 
Committee. 
5.  The Committee considered the Bi ll and heard a presentation by the S ecretary, Legislative Department, 
Ministry of Law and Justice on the 10th September, 2004. 
6.  The Committee heard oral evidence of 36 individu als/organisations/institutions/ experts including some 
Government Offices and PSUs, viz. MTNL, Railways Board, CPWD, HPCL, ONGC etc. who had been 
handling major arbitration cases. Th e Committee also heard the views of many eminent legal luminaries in 
Chennai and Hyderabad to have a better appreciation of the subject. Dr. Robert Briner, Chairman, International 
Court of Arbitration, International Chamber of Commerce, Paris also deposed before the Committee. 
7.  Contacts were established with the major international arbitration centres, namely the Singapore 
International Arbitration Centre, Hongkong International Arbitration Centre, the London Court of International 
Arbitration and International Court of Arbitration, Paris so as to collect information about the functioning of 
these Centres in the context of the idea mooted in the Committee on setting up institutionalized arbitration of 
world class standard. A proposal was also initiated to hold video conferencing between the Members of the 
Committee and the authorities of major international arbitration centres to exchange views and ideas on the 
subject and also to have first hand information about functioning of institutionalized arbitration. Although the 
proposed video conferencing did not materialise due to constraints of time, SIAC, HKIAC, LCIA responded to 
the queries of the Committee. The Committee also sought Legislative Department’s response on the 
suggestions made by the witnesses before the Committee.
