terrorism, cyber-crimes, corruption and many others and we cannot afford to have such a premier agency
understaffed and struggling with resource crunch. The Committee expresses its dismay over the existing
state of affairs in the C.B.I. To overcome the perennial problem of vacancies in the CBI, the Committee
recommends that the Government may consider making direct recruitment (in some proportion) at Group
'A' level in the agency through UPSC Civil Services Examination. Government may also consider making
terms of deputation to CBI more attractive so that officers from the State Police Forces, Central Para
Military Forces, Intelligence Bureau, etc. are tempted to join CBI on deputation.
(Para 3.17)
Action Taken
6.1. The earlier provision of direct recruitment of Dy. SP (Group ' A') through UPSC has been done
away on the recommendations of the Committee constituted in this regard after due consultations with
UPSC. Keeping in view the functional requirements of CBI, a Limited Departmental Competitive Examination
(LDCE) has been introduced to appoint officers at Dy. SP level.
6.2. New RRs have been notified for the Sr. Police Post in CBI in 2013 to ensure not only professionalism
in CBI but also to improve career progression of the departmental officers who are inducted at the level
of SI as direct recruit officers.
For the better career progression of the direct recruits SIs as well as to infuse fresh dynamic personnel
in the grade of Dy. SP, 10% quota has been provided for LDCE in the RRs.
6.3. SIs and Inspector are eligible to become Dy. SP through the LDCE route after putting in only five
years of service. Thus, the more meritorious among them would become Dy. SP.
6.4. This also ensures sufficient eligible officers are available in the feeder grade for promotion to the
rank of Dy. SP in CBI against the 80% quota for promotion prescribed in RR of Dy. SP.
6.5. If direct recruitment at the level of Dy. SP (Group 'A') is to be done through UPSC, it will not only
affect career progression of these officers but also bring frustration amongst them. Moreover, it will
affect promotion of eligible officers due to limited number of posts earmarked to direct recruitment at
the level of Dy. SP.

21
6.6. Hence, direct recruitment in CBI is kept only at the level of SI who would have sufficient experience
as IO before becoming eligible to hold supervisory ranks and keeping in view their career progression.
6.7. Efforts are also made to induct officers from other services i.e. Central Government organized
Group „A' Services, including services namely Indian Economic Services; Directorate of Enforcement;
Serious Fraud Investigation Office; Narcotics Control Bureau; Indian Revenue Service; Indian Customs
and Central Excise Services other than IPS, having specialization in different fields as per provision in
Rs.
Further Observation
6.8. The Committee is of the view that the CBI must ensure adequate staffing in order to deal
with the rising burden of investigations. However, the Government was not forthcoming regarding
measures it has taken for filling up of vacant positions. The Committee accordingly recommends
that proactive steps must be undertaken to fill up the existing vacancies in a time bound manner.
Recommendation/Observation
7.0. The CBI in its submission before the Committee stated that one of the major reasons why investigators
do not come on deputation to CBI is the lack of available housing. The overall housing satisfaction is
very low at pan India level and especially in Delhi where the Head Quarter is situated. As informed by
the Agency itself, even after proposed construction/acquisition of new quarters the satisfaction level
would remain substantially low in future also. Accordingly, the Committee recommends enhancing
significantly the allocation for acquiring land and building staff quarters of CBI at Delhi and other
locations, to bring the satisfaction level up to somewhere near to the level prescribed by the Ministry
of Urban Development. The Committee also expresses its dissatisfaction over failure of CBI to utilize
fully funds earmarked for housing for its personnel and desires that CBI should ensure that funds
allocated for the purpose are fully utilized by it. (Para 3.19)
Action Taken
7.1. To improve the housing satisfaction level, a proposal to build 586 quarters at Maidangarhi has been
sanctioned at a cost of ` 261.16 Crores by the Government on 29.03.2017. This will improve the housing
satisfaction from present 13% to 36%.
7.2. Construction of residential quarters will be completed in Tiruvananthapuram, Shillong, Goa in this
financial year.
Further Observation
7.3. The Committee observes that even with the construction of additional quarters, a huge gap
would still remain between the actual satisfaction level and that prescribed under the Ministry
of Urban Development norms. Therefore, the Committee reiterates that the fund allocation for
acquiring land and building staff quarters of CBI at Delhi and other locations should be significantly
enhanced, to bring the satisfaction level up to somewhere near to the level prescribed by the
Ministry of Urban Development. Further, CBI should also ensure that funds allocated for the
purpose are fully utilized.

22
CENTRAL ADMINISTRATIVE TRIBUNAL (CAT)
Recommendation/Observation
8.0. The Committee notes from the submission made by CAT that it has a requirement of additional
Benches at four places viz. Jabalpur, Cuttack, Jaipur and Lucknow, as only one Divisional Bench is
sanctioned at these places. Absence of any of the two members viz. Judicial and Administration hampers
the work of the Tribunal. There have been PILs filed in the concerned High Courts at these places where
a Bench could not be made functional for want of either of Members due to various reasons. The
Committee is of the view that if need for additional Bench exists at these places, these need to be set
up early so that Central Government employees get quick justice at these places. (Para 3.26)
Action Taken
8.1. CA T's proposal for creation of additional benches was examined earlier by DoPT and was not
agreed to after considering it on the ground of functional requirement and financial implications involved
in creation of Additional Benches. The yearly institution of cases during the last five years at these four
Benches were not justifying the creation of an additional Bench as the same were almost equal to or less
than the number of cases supposed to be disposed of yearly by a Division Bench as per the norms
stipulated by CAT itself. As per the norms stipulated by CAT, a Division Bench has to dispose of 5 cases
per day and 7 cases per day by Single Member Bench i.e. during 215 working days of a year, this comes
out to 1075 to 1505 cases yearly.
8.2. The court cases/PILs filed in the concerned High Courts at these places where a Bench could not
be made functional is due to delay in finalization in selection process for the year 2016. For the time
being it can be redressed by posting Members from other Benches by CAT. Creation of additional Bench
is not a solution when there is no Member therein. The situation will improve once the selection process
for the year 2016 is completed.
Further Observation
8.3. The Committee takes note of the reply. It, however, reiterates that proper infrastructure
in terms of physical as well as human should be provided to the CAT, to achieve the desired level
of performance. Present pace of efforts to fill up vacancies is inadequate and an effective
mechanism should be evolved for timely filling of vacancies. Further, the Committee may be
informed about the timelines for filling up of vacancies in the CAT.
Recommendation/Observation
9.0. The Committee has been informed that about 41,849 cases (as on 31/01/2017) are pending before
various benches of CAT. Out of which about 3,823 are pending for more than five years and about
10,007 are pending for 3-5 years. This is a substantial number. The Committee feels that it is imperative
upon the CAT to make concerted efforts so as to reduce the pendency substantially. In addition, the
Government should also make sustained efforts to streamline the service rules so that there is minimum
litigation; the internal grievance redressal mechanism within the respective Departments needs to be made

23
more robust to command the faith of the employees; and a mechanism be evolved so that many of the
cases in service matters can be settled within the system itself so that minimal number of cases go to
Tribunal. (Para 3.27)
Action Taken
9.1. Since 1985 about 7,42,036 cases have been instituted till February, 2017 and approximately 7,00,066
cases have already been disposed of, which is about 94.33%. During the last five years (2012-16)
1,41,161 cases were instituted and 1,24,101 were disposed of. As regards the reasons for pendency are
concerned, it is pertinent to mention here that the cases instituted within one year are not considered
to be a part of the arrears as these cases are in circulation for completion of the service and pleadings.
In so far as the pendency of cases ripe for hearing are concerned, the primary and perhaps the main
reason is huge number of vacancies in the Tribunal across the board. It is also to be placed on record
that the functioning of the Tribunal is different than other regular Courts where Benches can be
constituted by any two judges. Here in the Tribunal, a Division Bench could only be constituted of one
Judicial and one Administrative Member. Thus, the deficiency in either category hampers the functioning
of the Tribunal.
9.2. As regards evolving a mechanism to resolve the service matters in departments is concerned, it
would be appropriate if the judgment/order implemented in one case is made applicable to all similarly
situated persons which would surely reduce the number of cases to a large extent.
Further Observation
9.3. The Committee takes note of the reply. Further, as pointed out by the Committee and
endorsed by the CAT, huge number of vacancies in the Tribunal is the principal contributing
factor in rising level of pendency. The DoPT should therefore, take proactive measures for
initiating action for filling the anticipated vacancies in the CAT well in advance.
9.4. The CAT has made an important suggestion for reducing litigation that ''the judgment/order
implemented in one case is made applicable to all similarly situated persons". The Committee
is in agreement with the opinion given by the CAT. The Committee, however, feels that the
suggested action lies with the DoPT. The Committee would like to know whether the CAT has
ever approached the DoPT in this regard. What was their response along with difficulties, if any,
faced in implementing this suggestion. The Committee also impresses upon the DoPT to furnish
its comments on feasibility of implementing the suggestion of the CAT.
UNION PUBLIC SERVICE COMMISSION (UPSC)
Recommendation/Observation
10.0.  As previously discussed in the report (Para 3.6 and 3.7) the Committee is constrained to refer to
the submissions made by the various organizations/ institutions within the jurisdiction of the DoPT, such
as, the CBI, CIC, CVC, LBSNAA, ISTM, etc. pointing to the existence of a large number of vacancies
having remained unfilled in those organizations for a number of years and observes that if large number
of the vacancies in the organizations under the Department of Personnel and Training itself are remaining
unfilled for a number of years, the situation in other organizations of the Government of India would

24
be worse. The Committee, therefore, feels that the DoPT should in consultation with the recruiting
agencies like UPSC and SSC, evolve a mechanism for timely filling of vacancies in all organizations
of the Government. (Para 3.38)
Action Taken

year.
10.2.In regard to Section Officer post, 50% of the posts are filled through Limited Departmental
Competitive Examination (LDCE) and 50% of posts through promotion. In so far as LDCE is concerned,
results of SO-LDCE, 2015 have not yet been declared due to ongoing litigation in Delhi High Court and
also promotion to the post of Section Officer is not taking place due to ongoing litigation on 'own merit'

10.3.As mentioned above, due to pending litigation in Supreme Court on 'own merit' case, promotion to

10.4. CS-II Division of DoPT posts CSSS personnel to UPSC and CIC (only Group-A officers of CSSS)
directly. The sanctioned strength and vacancies position of CSSS in UPSC is as under:

25
completion of mandatory training, candidates are nominated to various cadre units including DoPT, after

10.12. In spite of efforts undertaken by the Deptt. as stated above, there are still huge vacancies
existing in the Government of India. The Committee, therefore, reiterates that the DoPT should,
in consultation with the recruiting agencies like UPSC and SSC, evolve a mechanism for timely
filling of vacancies in all organizations of the Government.
CENTRAL INFORMATION COMMISSION (CIC)
Recommendation/Observation
11.0. The CIC was established in the year 2005 and even after a decade of its establishment, the CIC
is severely understaffed. As per the information provided by the Commission, against a sanctioned
strength of 160 only 25 personnel are on permanent basis and rest are working on ad-hoc basis. Even
after Recruitment Rules are framed the appointments have not been made. The Committee expresses its
dismay over manning of the Commission's Secretariat through ad-hoc and temporary appointments and
strongly recommends that appointments of regular employees are done at the earliest, so that Commission's
working is made more responsive and accountable. (Para 3.54)
Action Taken
11.1. So far the Central Information Commission is concerned; there are 160 sanctioned posts in various
categories as on 3.02.2017 out of which 16 posts of MTS are sanctioned on outsourcing basis. Out of
the remaining 144 posts, 51 posts have been filled up by regular officers and staff. Remaining posts have
been filled up either through Consultants (Retd. Govt. Officers) or through outsourced staff.
11.2. So far as, action taken to fill up the vacancies on regular basis, is concerned, it is submitted that
the Recruitment Rules of various posts in the CIC had been notified in April - June, 2012. Subsequently,

26
advertisements have been issued by the CIC for filling up of various posts in July 2012, July 2013,
August 2014, January 2015, February 2016 and August 2016. Indents had been placed to the Staff
Selection Commission for direct recruitment on 08.12.2014, 06.01.2015 and 17.03.2015 for filling up
vacant posts of 30 Upper Division Clerk, 5 Assistants and 8 Stenographers Grade D. In first phase,
dossiers of 15 UDCs and 5 Assistants had been allocated to the Central Information Commission by the
Staff Selection Commission, out of which only 5 Assistants and 7 UDCs had joined the Commission in
February/May, 2016. Eight UDCs had not reported. In second phase dossiers of 15 UDCs and 8
Stenographers Grade 'D' have been received. 8 UDCs and 8 Stenographer Grade 'D' have joined the
Commission after completion of pre-appointment formalities. Remaining 7 UDCs and 7 Steno 'D' are
likely to join in the coming months.
11.3. DoPT has also encadred 19 posts in different categories for posting of officer and staff in the
Commission. Against these posts 1 Deputy Secretary, 1 Section Officer, 5 Assistants, 1 PA and 3
Stenographer Grade 'D' have been posted so far.
Further Observation
11.4. Inspite of the efforts mentioned by the Commission, the CIC is woefully under staffed and
therefore, they have to resort to  ad-hoc and temporary appointments. The Committee, therefore, reiterates
that appointments of regular employees should be made at the earliest.
DEPARTMENT OF ADMINISTRATIVE REFORMS AND PUBLIC GRIEV ANCES
Public Grievance Redressal and Public Service Delivery
Recommendation/Observation
12.0. Dealing with the grievances of citizen effectively is one of the core components of Good Governance.
CPGRAMS is a good initiative of the Government for redressal of citizen grievances. However, public
at large, particularly those who are living in rural and far-flung areas needs to be made aware of
existence of such grievance redressal system. The Committee, therefore, recommends that this system of
Public Grievance Redressal (CPGRAMS) should be publicized in mass media in vernacular languages,
so that common people become aware of availability of such avenue for redressal of their grievances
against the Government organisations. (Para 3.76)
Action Taken
12.1. Full page advertisements have been issued in the past in leading National and Regional newspapers
including vernacular on Public Grievance Redress Mechanism on 1.10.2011 and 20.3.2012. Issue of a
fresh advertisement in the coming months is under consideration.
Further Observation
12.2. The Public Grievance Redressal Mechanism (CPGRAMS) of the DARPG has evolved into
an effective platform for redressal of public grievances related to the Central Government.
However, people are not aware of availability of such a mechanism. Thus, there is a need for
giving wider publicity of this mechanism in mass media. Last time such an advertisement was
issued was way back in the year 2011-12 and no publicity has been done thereafter. The DARPG

27
should move beyond such tokenism and undertake aggressive mass media campaign to advertise
this grievance redressal mechanism. The Committee therefore, strongly reiterates that Public
Grievance Redressal Mechanism (CPGRAMS) should be publicized on a large scale and adequate
funds should be allotted for this. To start with, it should be regularly advertized through public
media viz. Doordarshan, All India Radio including FM channels.

REPORT
The Action Taken Report of the Committee deals with the action taken by the Ministry of Law and
Justice on the recommendations/observations of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee
on Personnel, Public Grievances, Law and Justice in its Ninety-first Report on the Demands for Grants
(2017-18) of the Ministry. The Report was presented to Rajya Sabha and laid on the Table of Lok Sabha
on the 15th March, 2017.
2. The Action Taken Replies of Legislative Department, Department of Legal Affairs, Department of
Justice, Ministry of Law and Justice in respect of the recommendations contained in the above mentioned
Report were received on 13th June, 28th September and 9th October, 2017, respectively. Replies of the
Departments have been categorised as follows:
Chapter-I : The recommendations/observations which have been accepted by the Ministry i.e., in
respect of para 3.9 of the Report. The Committee is pleased to note that the Ministry has accepted
its recommendations.
Chapter-II : The recommendations/observations which the Committee does not desire to pursue in
view of the replies given by the Ministry i.e., in respect of paras 5.7 and 6.22 of the Report. The
Committee has accepted the explanations furnished by the Ministry and does not wish to pursue
them further as of now.
Chapter-III : The recommendations/observations in respect of which Committee has not accepted
replies given by the Ministry i.e., with regard to paras 2.9, 3.6, 4.15, 5.4, 5.10, 5.16, 5.17, 5.20,
5.23, 6.15, 6.25, 6.29, 6.31 and 6.32, of the Report. The Committee expresses its concern for not
accepting the recommendations of the Committee dealt with in Chapter - III of this Report and
reiterates its recommendations.
Chapter-IV : The recommendations/observations on which final replies of the Ministry of Law and
Justice have not been received. The Committee expresses its deep concern that it did not receive
the replies from the Legislative Department/Election Commission in respect of Committee's
recommendations vide Para Nos. 4.0 to 4.26 except para 4.15, 6.8 and 6.16. Similarly, the reply
of Department of Justice was not received in respect of Committee recommendation vide Para 7.2.
The Committee desires that Ministry should furnish action taken report in respect of recommendations
mentioned in Chapter - IV without any further delay.

CHAPTER - I
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS WHICH HAVE BEEN
ACCEPTED BY THE MINISTRY
LEGISLATIVE DEPARTMENT INSTITUTE OF LEGISLATIVE DRAFTING AND RESEARCH (ILDR)
Recommendation/Observation
1. The Committee observes that the Institute has been in existence for almost three decades now and
substantial amount of public fund already spent on it. It would, therefore, be useful for the Department
to get a third party evaluation made of the quality of training being imparted at the Institute and the
extent to which training at the Institute has resulted in improved legislative drafting skills, so that
shortcomings, if any, could be removed and Institute involves into a globally reputed centre for legislative
drafting. (Para 3.9)
Action Taken
1.1. As regards the Secretarial staff and infrastructure of ILDR, the same are being audited on regular
intervals by the K.B.S. Certifying Agency as part and process of the ISO 2001-2008 Certificates which
have been awarded to the Institute. So far as imparting of training in legislative drafting is concerned,
the ILDR is imparting both theoretical as well as practical training with the assistance of serving and
retired draft persons. After the completion of the Basic Course and Appreciation Course in legislative
drafting, feedback is taken from the trainee officers and on the basis of inputs received, the quality of
training is improved. Further, the very existence of this Department which prepares the draft Bills and
scrutinizes the subordinate legislations of all the Ministries and Departments of the Central Governments
under the respective Acts administered by them is itself an evaluation that the ILDR is competent to
impart training in legislative drafting. However, if the ILDR receives any suggestions for its improvements,
the same will be adopted for the improvement in training in legislative drafting in the ILDR.
Further Observation
1.2. The Committee takes note of the reply. The Committee also appreciates the activities of
ILDR and is of the view that it should forge Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) with similar
institutions around the world to keep pace with the best global practices in legislative drafting.
The Committee also feels that ILDR should be developed as an institution of national importance
and should play active role in imparting training on legislative drafting to personnel of developing
countries.

- was utilized during the year 2016-17 and `19,52,993/- was left during the aforesaid financial year. It
is mentioned that `10.64 Crore is allocated for the financial year 2017-18. This amount will be utilized
during the financial year 2017-18. It may further be stated that this Wing has projected the budget for
the financial year 2017-18 as per genuine requirement. In so far as Vidhi Sahitya Prakashan is concerned,
proposals are under consideration to fill the vacant post in different grades. Measures have been taken
to purchase required items/goods for office. Initiative has already been taken to pay the pending bills with
the government press for printing the Uchhcha Nayalaya Patrikas/Uchchtama Nayalaya Patrikas. Proposals
of domestic travel under propagation of Hindi are under consideration.
Further Observation
2.3. The Committee notes that the meagre funds allocated to Official Languages Wing and Vidhi
Sahitya Prakashan in BE (2016-2017) were further reduced at the RE (2016-2017) stage. Official
Languages Wing have submitted in their reply that they were not able to fully utilise the funds
allocated at the RE (2016-2017) stage but have not cited any reasons for the same. The ATR of
Vidhi Sahitya Prakashan is completely silent on the extent of utilization of funds allocated to
them in RE (2016-2017), which they ought to have provided. However, they had an unutilized
amount of Rs 1.34 Cr up to January, 2017. The Committee desires that it be informed as to what
extent Official Languages Wing was able to utilize the amounts sanctioned to them in BE (2017-
2018) and Vidhi Sahitya Prakashan in RE (2016-2017) and BE (2017-2018). The Committee,
therefore, recommends that these spending units should seek funds from the Ministry of Finance
on the basis of their realistic requirements and closely monitor their expenditure.
ELECTION COMMISSION OF INDIA
Voting Rights of Domestic Migrants
Recommendation/Observation
3. According to Census 2011 and National Sample Survey Organisation (NSSO), migrants constitute
about 30 percent of the country's population and also of the total working force. The Economic Survey
(2016-17) also noted that annual migration in the country increased to 9.00 million in 2016 from 3.30
million in 2011. As per the existing law they can cast their vote in the constituencies where they are
registered as voters. During the elections they are not able to cast their vote at their place of work or
in their constituency as they are constantly on move from one place to another in search of better

8
livelihood. The Commission during the Demands for Grants (2017-18) informed that a Committee was
constituted to look into the issues of domestic migrant and it has already given its recommendations,
which has been forwarded to Legislative Department, to enable them to cast their vote at their place
of work or business. The Committee, accordingly, recommends the Commission and the Legislative
Department to expedite the matter so that domestic migrants are not deprived of their right to vote which
is a basic right of every citizen in the country. (Para 4.15)
Action Taken
3.1. The Commission has forwarded a copy of the 'Report of Committee of Officers on Domestic
Migrants' which was submitted by the Commission before the Hon'ble Supreme Court of India in W.P.
No. 1005 of 2013. It was also forwarded to the Ministry of Law and Justice, vide Commissions letter
dated 29.05.2017.
3.2. The Legislative Department has referred to the above report of the Commission and has forwarded
their comments on the recommendations contained in the report. They have further submitted that the
whole idea of putting in place alternative modes of voting for domestic migrants is contingent on (i) the
development of fool-proof system for two-way postal ballot; and (ii) consultation with stakeholders by
the Election Commission. Therefore, no actionable proposal is pending in the Legislative Department.
However, the Election Commission has been separately requested to examine the matter further and
come-up with definite proposals for consideration of the Government.
Further observation
3.3. The Committee is of the view that voting rights of domestic migrants are as important as
for any other citizen and delay on the part of the Department/Election Commission of India is
a serious issue as it deprives millions of citizens of exercising their democratic right to vote. The
Committee, therefore, reiterates that the Commission and the Legislative Department should
expedite the matter so that domestic migrants are not deprived of their right to vote.
DEPARTMENT OF LEGAL AFFAIRS
Shortage of Officers in the Department
Recommendation/observation
4. The Committee expresses its serious concern over the acute shortage of officers in the Department.
The Department needs to urgently address the causes responsible for this state of affairs and ensure that
vacancies of officers are filled up at the earliest. (Para 5.4)
Action Taken
4.1. Department of Legal Affairs is making continuous efforts to fill up its vacant posts and vehemently
pursuing the matter with the recruiting agencies i.e. Union Public Service Commission (UPSC) and Staff
Selection Commission (SSC). Pursuant to persistent efforts, all the three posts of Additional Secretaries
have been filled by promotion. Three Joint Secretary & Legal Advisers have joined this Department by
direct recruitment. Besides, proposal for filling up of 6 posts of Joint Secretary & Legal Adviser is under
active consideration of this Department and the matter has been taken up with the UPSC for obtaining
of NOC. Further, in pursuance of the recruitment process for two posts of Additional Legal Adviser in
DR quota, fresh recommendation from UPSC has been solicited and the same is awaited for these two
posts. In addition to this, a proposal has been approved by the Hon'ble Minister of Law & Justice for

9
diversion of 8 vacancies of Additional Legal Adviser falling under Promotion Quota to Direct Recruitment
Quota. This, however, requires approval of Department of Expenditure for revival of these posts as the
same have come under deemed abolition. Approval of Department of Expenditure to this effect has been
sought. After approval, a proposal will be taken up with the UPSC for filling up of 8 vacancies of
Additional Legal Adviser on DR basis. Similarly, the Staff Selection Commission (SSC) has conveyed that
the recruitment process for 08 posts of Assistant (Legal) is in final stage and the same would be over
in 2-3 months' time and thereafter the names of selected candidates would be recommended for appointment.
Further observation
4.2. The Committee notes that the reply of the Department only provides information regarding
status of recruitment to various posts in the Department and is completely silent on the causes
responsible for the shortage of manpower in the Department. The Committee wishes to be
apprised of the latest post wise vacancy position in the Department, as well as causes responsible
for the shortage of manpower and remedial actions being taken by the Department to evolve a
mechanism for timely filling of vacancies so that functioning of the Department is not hampered.
LA W COMMISSION OF INDIA
Recommendation/Observation
5. The Committee is of the view that vacancies of officers in the Law Commission of India need to
be filled-up urgently to ensure efficient and smooth functioning of the Commission. The Committee
reiterates its recommendation contained in Seventy-fifth and Eighty-fourth Reports on the Demands for
Grants (2015-16 and 2016-17) and suggests that all the agencies like concerned Department, UPSC and

Commission of India was taken up the Union Public Service Commission (UPSC) and Department of
Personnel & Training (DoP&T). The UPSC and DoP&T have suggested to amend the recruitment Rules.
The Proposal for amendments in the Indian Legal Service Rules, 1957, is under consideration and

Further observation
5.2. The Committee takes note of the reply and recommends that the decision on the proposal
for amending the Indian Legal Service Rules, 1957 should be expedited so that the recruitment

the Rules ibid to the Committee. The Committee also notes that the reply of the Department

INCOME TAX APPELLATE TRIBUNAL (ITAT)
Recommendation/Observation
6. The Committee expresses its serious concern and anguish over the pendency existing in Income Tax
Appellate Tribunal. The Committee notes that between the years 2004 and 2010, pendency was substantially

10
reduced but thereafter, disposal rate has not been commensurate with the disposal rate of the year 2004-
05 and, therefore pendency, in the Tribunal again has increased to an alarming level. This is a serious
reflection on the state of affairs existing in the Tribunal and the Committee recommends that the
Department should urgently review the reasons for this state of affairs and take remedial measures
urgently so that the pendency shows substantial improvement. (Para 5.16)
Action Taken
6.1. Income Tax Appellate Tribunal has reported that during the year 2015-16, 39 New Members
(Judicial/Accountant) have joined ITAT and it took some time for them to settle down. ITAT has, in this
regard, also issued necessary instructions to its Benches to scrutinize and identify cases (group and small
matter) which are covered by decisions of ITAT, High Courts and the Supreme Court and post / list them
on priority basis. The Bar has also been requested to bring to the notice of ITAT, all such covered cases
for out of turn posting. Besides, Search & Seizure cases and appeals u/s 263 are being given priority
in their disposal. The ITAT has also introduced use of information technology for early disposal of appeal
by introducing e-court i.e. hearing through video conferencing. Such stations where e-courts have been
made functional are Delhi-Jabalpur, Ahmedabad-Rajkot and Mumbai-Nagpur. Recently, Kolkata-Guwahati
has been linked. Efforts are also on for linking Ahmedabad-Surat and Kolkata-Ranchi. ITAT has assured
that all best possible efforts shall be made so that gradually pendency of appeals is reduced considerably
in near future. Department of Legal Affairs, on its part, has also urged, President, ITAT to put in place
an effective mechanism to increase monthly disposal rate by each Member of the Tribunal, with a view
to reduce pendency in ITAT.
Further observation
6.2. The Committee notes that the reply is silent on whether the Department has reviewed the
reasons for declining rate of disposal of cases by ITAT, resulting in huge pendency. The reply only
states the measures being taken by ITAT in an effort to reduce pendency. The Committee would
like to be apprised of the reasons for decline in the disposal rates by ITAT and also whether all
the above measures undertaken by ITAT are proving effective to reduce pendency and, if so, to
what extent. The Committee observes that the disposal rate in 2015-16 was higher than that of
in the years from 2009-10 to 2014-15, it therefore, fails to understand the reasoning given by
ITAT that increase in pendency is due to the fact that during the year 2015-16, 39 New Members
joined ITAT and it took some time for them to settle down.
6.3. Further, as per the Annual Report 2016-17 of the Ministry of Law & Justice, out of the
sanctioned strength of 126 Members of Tribunals, 25 posts were lying vacant. The Committee,
therefore, recommends that proactive measures should be taken to fill all the existing vacancies
expeditiously as this would also improve the disposal rate in ITAT. The Committee would also like
to be apprised whether the President, ITAT has put in place any mechanism to increase monthly
disposal rate by each Member of the Tribunal. The Committee also feels that the Department
should develop some rating mechanism for ITAT Benches and an annual exercise of rating each
Bench should be followed to gauge their performance and may be suitably reflected in the Annual
Report of the Ministry.

11
Recommendation/Observation
7. The Committee also recommends that the Government should seriously review continuance of such
Tribunals which have become non-functional or have very few cases. The Government should also
comprehensively address the problem of overlapping jurisdiction of the Tribunal to ensure efficient
functioning of the Tribunals. (Para 5.17)

(iv) The Appellate Tribunal for Foreign Exchange with the Appellate Tribunal under the Smugglers
and Foreign Exchange Manipulators (Forfeiture of Property) Act, 1976.
(v) The National Highways Tribunal with the Airport Appellate Tribunal.
(vi) The Cyber Appellate Tribunal with the Telecom Dispute Settlement and Appellate Tribunal.
(vii) The Airport Economic Regulatory Authority Tribunal with the Telecom Dispute Settlement and
Appellate Tribunal.
(viii) The Competition Appellate Tribunal with the National Company Law Appellate Tribunal
Further Observation
7.2. The Committee notes the reply and feels that merging of tribunals was sine qua non  to cut wasteful
expenditure of government and speed-up disposal of cases. However, the Committee notes that the reply
of the Department is silent on the measures taken/ proposed to be taken by the Government to address
the problem of overlapping jurisdiction of the Tribunals.
INDIAN LA W INSTITUTE (ILI)
Recommendation/Observation
8. Indian Law Institute being a premier legal research institute which has been granted deemed
university status in the year 2004, should strive to become a self-sustaining Institute imparting high
quality of legal education and research and avoid being a permanent drag on public funds. It is not
befitting the status of this premier legal Institute to raise any part of its resources by renting a portion
of its building. It should ideally use all its resources only for imparting legal education and research and
raise funds from them. However, in order to make it self-sustaining, if Government funds are to be
provided for a limited period, the Committee recommends that such funds should be provided.
(Para 5.20)
Action Taken
8.1. The Ministry of Law and Justice shares the concern of the Committee on making Indian Law
Institute (ILI) self-sustainable. As per the provisions of a loan agreement with the Ministry, ILI has leased

12
out space other than the Ground floor to the Ministry and receives rent in lieu thereof. The institute
otherwise generates revenue from course fee, sale of publication, etc. and in total earns ` 4 Crore approx
annually. In addition, Department of Legal Affairs provides recurring grant to ILI to meet its expenses
on salary, and other administrative expenditure. This Department's endeavor is to provide all deficit funds
to ILI to make it self-sustainable. In last three years, ILI has been extended grants amounting to `
7,02,72,250/- (2014-15, 2015-16, and 2016-17). In the current financial year, beside recurring grant, a
proposal to fund additional requirement of ILI in lieu of implementation of the recommendations of the
Seventh Central Pay Commission is also under active consideration. On its part, the Institute is taking
necessary steps for filling up their faculty positions with a view to improving research activities and to
enhance the stature of the Institute at par with International Standards. Further, the Institute is exploring
new avenues for expansion of its activities, if required by allotment of additional space and enhancement
of its Corpus Fund.
Further Observation
8.2. The Committee is of the view that it is not befitting the status of this premier legal Institute
to raise any part of its resources by renting a portion of its building. It should use all its
resources only for academic/research activities and raise funds by expanding these activities. The
Committee notes that as per the submissions of Director, ILI during DFG (2017-2018), almost
50% of posts in ILI were vacant. The Committee, therefore, recommends that vacant positions
in ILI should be filled-up immediately so that it is able to expand its activities and move in the
direction of becoming a self-sustaining Institute. The Committee also desires to be apprised of
the status of the recruitment process in ILI. The Committee also reiterates the recommendation
made in its Eighty-fourth report for statutory back-up to the Institute.
NOTARIES APPOINTMENT
Recommendation/Observation
9. The Committee is of the view that Notaries are important link in the judicial system and provide
cost effective services to public for various basis services viz., verification, authentication, certification
of documents etc. in the country. The Committee is of the opinion that the process of appointment of
Notaries needs to be further streamlined and made more robust so that competent persons are appointed
as Notaries. (Para 5.23)
Action Taken
9.1. Department of Legal Affairs is in agreement with the observation made by the Hon'ble Parliamentary
Committee that the competent person may be appointed as Notaries. In this regard, it is submitted that
to judge the competency of person for appointment as a Notary, Interview Board, is constituted under
Rule 7 of the Notaries Rule, 1956. As per Rule 7 of the Notaries Rules, the Interview Board shall consist
of the officers dealing with legal matters and the Chairperson of the Board shall be an officer not below
the rank of Joint Secretary or Law Officer. The Interview Board, after accessing the suitability of person,
submits its recommendation and after taking into the consideration of the recommendation of the
Interview Board, Notaries are appointed. To streamline the process for appointment of Notaries, the
Department of Legal Affairs has started to accept online applications for appointment of Notaries. Further

13
action to improve the process of appointment of Notaries is envisaged through continuous and periodic
assessment of current procedures.
Further Observation
9.2. The Committee appreciates the initiative of accepting online applications for Notaries but
it still feels that the process of appointment of Notaries needs to be further streamlined. The
Department may consider awarding points on some broad parameters to short list applicants for
Notaries interview and publish the result online so that candidates may know the fate of their
application. They may be kept informed at various stages of the appointment process and the said
process should be time bound. The Committee would also like to be apprised of the periodicity
of assessment of the procedure of appointment of Notaries since the Notification of the Notaries
Rule, 1956.
DEPARTMENT OF JUSTICE
National Legal Services Authority (NALSA)
Recommendation/Observation
10. NALSA has an important role in making justice available to poor and marginalized section of the
society. The Committee, however, notes that the funds provided to the Authority are inadequate and
recommends that the Government should appropriately enhance Grants-in-aid made available to the
Authority. The Authority may also explore other avenues for raising resources for achieving its objectives.
The Committee, however, is not happy over the quality of legal services being made available under the
Scheme. There is need not only to provide legal services to the needy but also that the quality of legal
service provided is of a high standard. The Committee feels this is where the Authority falls short of the
expectations of the Committee and would like the Authority to concentrate on improving the quality of
legal services being provided by it. It may also consider suitably revising the fee paid to the advocates
who provide legal services under the Scheme. It should also make the system of empanelment of lawyers
for providing services under the Scheme more transparent, robust and accountable. (Para 6.15)
Action Taken
10.1.In order to improve the quality of legal services provided by the State Legal Services Authorities,
the National Legal Services Authority has recently taken measures addressing a procedure for selection
of panel lawyers, monitoring of cases assigned to them and enhancement of the fee payable to them.
Some of the steps taken are as follows:
(a) NALSA has enhanced the Lawyers fee for Panel Lawyers assigned to the Legal Aid applicants.
All the State Legal Services Authorities have been requested to take necessary steps to implement
the minimum fee structure as prescribed by NALSA.
(b) State Legal Services Authorities have also been requested to take steps for appointing remand
advocates in all the Magisterial Courts/Sessions Court, wherever required, and to fix their
honorarium at par with the retainer lawyers, as per the guidelines of NALSA. This is to ensure
that every undertrial prisoner gets legal assistance right from the first day of his production
in the court.
(c) NALSA has passed a resolution that in places where the monitoring committee has not been
constituted, as per Regulations 10 of NALSA (Free and Competent Legal Services) Regulations,
2010, the same shall be constituted at the earliest.

14
(d) As regards the appointment of efficient and committed Panel Lawyers, it may be stated that
a committee has been constituted by NALSA, comprising of Three Executive Chairpersons of
State Legal Services Authorities and two Chairperson of High Court Legal Services Committee,
to whom all the SLSA's shall give their suggestions for appointment of efficient and committed
panel lawyers.
(e) The committee in its first meeting has started preparing guidelines as to how the SLSAs to
empanel the lawyers so as to strengthen the core activity of providing of court based legal
aid.
(f) NALSA has prepared training modules for legal services lawyers which would better facilitate
the process of training of the panel lawyers. Two parts of the module have already been
released and are being utilised by the SLSAs. NALSA is already working on the third part.
NALSA is also training Master Trainers to conduct training as per the module in their respective
States.
(g) NALSA in partnership with Department of Justice and UNDP has introduced a new legal aid
scheme namely 'Tele Law'. This has been introduced in 1000 Gram Panchayats of UP and
Bihar. This scheme facilitates legal aid to marginalized persons through video conference/chat/
telephone at the Common Service Centres. Tele-law model is facilitating legal advice and
referral through expert panel lawyers placed with State Legal Service Authorities. As on date,
out of 2859 cases registered, legal advice has been rendered in 2098 cases. Most of the
beneficiaries are women, SC, ST and other marginalized persons.
(h) The Government has also introduced a Pro Bono Legal Service scheme for marginalized
persons. An online application procedure for interested lawyers to enroll has been launched at
doj.gov.in. As on date 158 advocates have enrolled in the portal.
(i) The Government is going to engage 227 Nyaya Mitras to be selected from retired judicial
officers as well as this Nyaya Mitras will be engaged in the district where there are large
number of 10 years old cases pending. This will also assist nearby litigants for speedy disposal
of their cases.
Further Observation
10.2. The Committee takes note of the reply and appreciates the initiatives of NALSA. The
Committee feels that a respectable fee to lawyers is a pre-requisite for a quality legal service
and accordingly, appreciates NALSA for enhancing fee of lawyers. The fee may also be revised
periodically. The Committee also appreciates the initiative of Tele-Law and feels that it will go
a long way in delivering justice to the marginalized sections, especially in underdeveloped and
backward regions of the country. The Committee notes that NALSA has constituted a committee
to whom all the SLSA's shall give suggestions for appointment of efficient and committed panel
lawyers and it would like to be apprised of the recommendations of this committee. However, the
Committee expresses its deep concern over under-utilization of funds by NALSA, leading to fund
reduction. Accordingly, the Committee impresses upon NALSA to fully utilize funds allocated to
it each year so that quality legal services are made available to poor and marginalized sections
of the society.

15
Recommendations/Observations
11. The Committee appreciates use of Information and Communication technologies in justice delivery
system for benefit of the litigants and court officials and to cut red-tapism, increase efficiency, transparency
and account-ability in the system. The Committee hopes the Department will make use of experiences
gained in Phase-I of the project, for robust and effective implementation of the Phase-II. The Committee
recommends that the Department should expedite the process of digitization and hardware installations
under the project and achieve targets set in a time-bound manner. The Committee further recommends
that periodic evaluations of the project be carried out so as to make timely intervention, if any, needed
for completion of the project, as scheduled. (Para 6.25)
Action taken/proposed to be taken by the Department
11.1.(1) Salient Features of the Project :
(a) Decentralised Implementation:  In Phase II of the eCourts Project, as designed by the
eCommittee of the Supreme Court of India and also approved by the Government of India,
the implementation of the Project has been decentralized to the High Courts for the Courts
falling under the jurisdiction of the particular High Court. Based on the technical specifications
finalised by the eCommittee in consultation with the Government of India, all the High Courts
have started the procurement of the hardware for their Courts.
(b) Direct Funds to High Courts: The funds of the eCourts Project have been transferred to
the High Courts by the Government of India to be expended by the High Courts for approved
activities of the Project.
(c) Cloud Architecture: The Case Information Software for District Courts is mandated to be
shifted to Cloud based architecture in Phase II of the eCourts Project.
(d) Litigants' Charter: 30 different services on 7 different e-platforms as referred in the Litigants'
Charter of eCourts Project, are aimed to be delivered by way of implementation of the Phase
II of the eCourts Project.
(e) Horizontal and Vertical Integration through National Judicial Data Grid : Though uniquely
identifying each and every case of Courts of all level through a CNR (Case Number Record)
number, it has been planned to establish horizontal and vertical integration of data of all the
Courts so that in case of inter se transfer of cases and filing of cases at higher level of Courts
against the orders/judgments of courts under those courts, there would be fetching of data
and status of the case horizontally and vertically respectively.
2. Activities so far in Phase II:
(a) Total budget of Phase II of eCourts project is `1670 crore. The duration of the project is four
years, i.e July 2019 or until the project is completed, whichever is later. The project sanction
notification was issued on 04.08.2015. So far `893.40 crore has been released by the
Government of India to various High Courts and other agencies towards implementation of
various project components. So far Utilization Certificates have been received for ` 225.48
crore only.

16
(b) Actual transfer of funds has started since January, 2016. Almost all High Courts have already
procured the required computer hardware i.e computers, printers, Display boards, etc., and
got them installed. LAN installation process is in progress. Procurement of Information Kiosks
are yet to be completed by many High Courts.
(c) Video Conferencing for remaining Court Complexes and Jails: The desktop based video
conferencing infrastructure has been established at 488 court complexes and 342 jails in Phase
I of the Project. The eCommittee now has decided to establish Video Conferencing facility at
the remaining 2768 Court Complexes and 958 Jails. During the current FY the Government
has released `64.33 crore to various High Courts for establishment of Video Conferencing
system.
(d) SMS based Case Information Services: Through the National Core Case Information Software
(NC CIS 1.1) and also the new CIS version 2.0, SMS services have been launched at majority
of the Court Complexes having leased line connectivity given in the eCourts Project. SMS is
sent to the lawyer/litigant whose mobile number is fed into the system on filing, registration,
listing and disposal of the case. Presently 886 Court Complexes out of total 2589 Computerised
Court Complexes are delivering SMS based services.
(e) Mobile Application for E-Courts :  NIC has developed a mobile based eCourts application to
render all services as presently available from website of ecourts.gov.in. The same was
released in August 2017. The mobile app has received a huge response from litigants, advocates
and other interested groups. In a short period of less than a month since it has been released
about one lakh users has downloaded the app. The app is available for Android and iOS
platforms.
(f) E-filing Application for High Courts and District Courts:  The eCommittee software
development team has developed an efiling application for High Courts and District Courts.
The application also offers integration with online payment gateways. Alerts through SMS and
Email are integrated in the application. It is under the process of security audit.
3. National eCourts Portal and National Judicial Data Grid (NJDG):
(a) National eCourts Portal:
(i) The e-Courts National portal (ecourts.gov.in), which was launched by Hon'ble the Chief
Justice of India on 7th August, 2013, provides cause-list, case status information and
order/judgments etc. in respect of more than 8.59 crore cases (pending and decided).
Presently, case information of about 2.52 Crores pending cases of subordinate judiciary
is disseminated through eCourts portal.
(ii) Almost all the District Courts in the country have launched their websites for the
convenience of litigants and others. All these websites are integrated with eCourts portal
i.e. ecourts.gov.in and case related information can be directly accessed using these
websites.
(b) National Judicial Data Grid i.e NJDG:
(i) The NJDG is a very powerful and useful tool which enables the High Court and the
District Judge to effectively monitor cases, including pendency and arrears. The e-Courts

17
National portal and NJDG also provide a number of statistical reports that can be used
as a judicial management information system. This portal is expected to play a key role
in bringing about judicial reforms.
(ii) Through NJDG, the figures of pendency of District Judiciary Courts across the country,
in aggregate for country and states as well as individual Court/Judge wise were left open
for being accessed by anyone visiting the National eCourts portal ecourts.gov.in.
(iii) This NJDG public access page, as available at ecourts.gov.in/services disseminates national
and state, district and court wise information about institution and disposal of last month
of cases and also the cases filed by senior citizens and women in the total pendency.
These statistics, which are being updated almost everyday by the respective Court
Complexes covered under the eCourts Project, show case pendency broken into Civil and
Criminal Cases segregated into age-wise categories of upto 2 years, between 2 to 5 years,
between 5 to 10 years and more than 10 years.
4 Change Management Exercise :
(i) Change Management exercise has been successfully implemented. All judicial officers in
the country have been trained in the use of Ubuntu Linux Operating System through 470
judicial officers who had been trained as Master Trainers as part of the Change Management
Programme conducted by the eCommittee. 222 of these master trainer judicial officers
have also been trained in the Case Information Software (CIS) 2.0 being implemented for
Courts across the country. Ubuntu Linux OS has been specially customized by the
eCommittee for the use in the laptops of the Judicial Officers and the Court Computers,
which has been widely appreciated by one and all.
(ii) About 480 CIS Master Trainers (District System Administrators) have been trained from
amongst the court staff in the use of the Case Information Software. These CIS Master
Trainers have trained more than 4000 System Administrators in the effective use of
computers and CIS. These CIS Trainer cum District System Administrator Court Officials
have also undergone a Refresher Training Programme conducted by the eCommittee in
the year 2014.
5. Digitization of Judicial Records:
As this component for District Judiciary was not a part of the approved activities in Phase
I of the eCourts Project, the same had been included and principally approved by the eCommittee
for Phase II of the eCourts Project. But during the financial approval process of the same at
Government level, this component has been shifted to 14th Finance Commission resources.
Accordingly, ` 752.50 Crore have been recommended in the 14th Finance Commission Report
towards scanning & digitization of case records. eCommittee has requested the High Courts
to pursue the State Governments for allocation of resources under 14th Finance Commission
for scanning and digitization of case records of subordinate judiciary.
6. Evaluation of the Project:
The evaluation of Phase-I of the project has been completed by National Council of Applied
Economic Research (NCAER). NCAER carried out an assessment study to evaluate the effect

18
of computerization in District and Subordinate Courts across the country. The NCAER assessment
study has found that the eCourts project has created awareness about computerization among
courts and about the application software, namely, case, information system among the important
stakeholders. The project has achieved more than 90% in ICT deployment in terms of asset
creation and the eCourts project was able to save time in work process through computerisation.
The Department floated an EOI-cum-RFP for Mid-term evaluation of eCourts Mission Mode
Project Phase-II during December, 2016; but did not attract eligible bidders. The Department

GRAM NYAYALAYAS
Recommendation/Observation
12. The Committee takes note of increased allocation by Rs 3 crore for Gram Nyayalayas in BE (2017-
18) over BE & RE (2016-17). The Committee, however , expresses its concern at the slow pace of
establishment of Gram Nyayalayas in the Country as only ten states have notified Gram Nyayalayas, and
out of these not a single Gram Nyayalayas is functional in the states of Karnataka, Jharkhand and Goa.
Uttar Pradesh, which has the highest population in the country, has only two functional Gram Nyayalayas.
The Committee, accordingly, recommends the Department to find reasons for slow implementation of the
project as also to study if Gram Nyayalayas which are functional serving the intended purpose and
inform the Committee as to how Government proposes to proceed with the establishment of Gram
Nyayalayas throughout the country. (Para 6.29)
Action Taken
12.1.In terms of Section 3 (1) of the Gram Nyayalayas Act, 2008, it is for the State Governments to
establish Gram Nyayalayas in consultation with the respective High Courts. As per information made
available by State Governments / High Courts, 320 Gram Nyayalayas have been notified so far by 11
States, out of these, 204 are operational in eight States at present, as per details given below:

12.2. The difficulties faced by States in setting up of Gram Nyayalayas were discussed in the meeting
of the Law/Home Secretaries and Registrar Generals of the High Courts held on 19 - 20 April, 2012.
One of the main reasons for the slow pace has been the request by the States for more financial
assistance. Besides, response of the Bar, reluctance of police officials and other State functionaries to
invoke jurisdiction of Gram Nyayalayas, non-availability of notaries and stamp vendors and more importantly,
problem of concurrent jurisdiction of regular courts, are other issues highlighted by the States which are
coming in the way of speedy operationalization of the scheme.
12.3.In the year 2011, the Indian Law Institute (ILI) was entrusted by the Department of Justice to
conduct a study on the effectiveness of functioning of Gram Nyayalayas in two states - Madhya Pradesh
and Rajasthan. The study concluded that Gram Nyayalayas in the states of Madhya Pradesh and Rajasthan
have not achieved the objectives of either speedy disposal or inexpensive justice for the poor. The Study
put forth a series of recommendations to improve the functioning of these Gram Nyayalayas. The
suggestions include:
(i) Establishment of Permanent Gram Nyayalayas: Gram Nyayalayas may be established in
every Panchayats at intermediate level or group of contiguous Panchayats at intermediate level
depending upon the number of disputes normally arise from that area. Whilst determining the
location of Gram Nyayalayas, the location of courts having parallel jurisdiction may also be
considered;
(ii) Infrastructure and Security: Separate building for the functioning of the Gram Nyayalayas
as well as for the accommodation of the Gram Nyayadhikaris  and other staff needs to be
constructed;
(iii) Creation of a regular cadre of Gram Nyayadhikaris: It is also imminent that a regular cadre
of Gram Nyayadhikari is created. Another suggestion was to make it a compulsory service
for a certain period for a newly recruited judicial officer to the regular cadre of First Class
Judicial Magistrate;
(iv) Training of Nyayadhikaris:  Apart from the legal and procedural requirements of Gram
Nyayalayas, training may also include the local language of the community amongst whom
they are posted;

20
(v) Jurisdiction of the Gram Nyayalayas  may be re-defined: In order to remove the ambiguities
regarding the jurisdiction of Gram Nyayalayas, the Act may be amended;
(vi) Creating awareness among various stakeholders: Suitable steps may be taken for creating
awareness among various stakeholders including the revenue and police officers.
12.4.  The report concluded that despite initial problems, institution of Gram Nyayalayas would succeed
if concrete, well planned and continuous efforts are made. The issues affecting operationalization of the
Gram Nyayalayas were discussed in the Conference of Chief Justices of High Courts and Chief Ministers
of the States on 7th April, 2013. It was decided in the Conference that the State Governments and High
Courts should decide the question of establishment of Gram Nyayalayas wherever feasible, taking into
account their local problems. The focus is on setting up Gram Nyayalayas in the Talukas where regular
courts have not been set up.
Further Observation
12.5. Despite the enhanced allocations to States under the 14th Finance Commission, the
Committee expresses its disappointment on the slow pace of development of Gram Nyayalayas
and impresses upon the Department, in consultation with State Governments, to initiate an all-
out effort to root out the hindrances affecting their establishment. The Committee is of the view
that delegation of responsibility to establish Gram Nyayalayas to High Courts and State
Governments in Conference of Chief Justices of High Courts and Chief Ministers of the States
since 2013 has not seen any heartening improvement. Accordingly, the Committee impresses
upon the Department to explore a tri-partite model so that expertise of the Department could
also be utilized in establishing Gram Nyayalayas.
12.6. The Committee also notes that the study conducted by Indian Law Institute (ILI) on the
effectiveness of functioning of Gram Nyayalayas in Madhya Pradesh and Rajasthan concluded
that despite initial problems, institution of Gram Nyayalayas would succeed if concrete, well
planned and continuous efforts are made. The Study put forth a series of recommendations to
improve the functioning of these Gram Nyayalayas; however, the reply of the Department is
silent on whether these recommendations have been implemented or not. The Committee desires
to be apprised of the action taken by the Department in this regard.
VACANCIES OF JUDGES IN HIGHER JUDICIARY
Recommendation/Observation
13. The Committee is concerned with the large number of vacancies of Judges in High Courts and
reiterates recommendations contained in Eighty-seventh Report on the Committee on the Inordinate Delay
in Filling up the Vacancies in the Supreme Court and High Courts". It further recommends that pending
finalization of supplemental Memorandum of Procedure/review of judgements/ Constitutional amendments,
appointments of Judges should continue as per hitherto existing practice as an ad-hoc measure so that
administration of justice does not suffer. (Para 6.31)
Action Taken
13.1. The appointment of Judges in the Supreme Court and High Courts is a continuous and collaborative
process of the Judiciary and Executive. While every effort is made to fill vacancies expeditiously,
vacancies keep on arising on account of retirement, resignation or elevation of Judges and increase in
Judge strength.

21
13.2. All appointments of Judges of Supreme Court and High Courts are being made as per the existing
procedure pending finalization of the revised Memorandum of Procedure. As per the existing procedure
the initiation of proposal for appointment of Judges in the Supreme Court vests with the Chief Justice
of India, while initiation of proposal for appointment of Judges in the High Courts vests with the Chief
Justice of the concerned High Court. As per the existing Memorandum of Procedure for appointment
of Judges of High Courts, the Chief Justice of the High Court is required to initiate the proposal for filling
up of vacancies of a Judge in a High Court six months prior to the occurrence of vacancies. However,
this timeline is rarely adhered to by the High Courts.
13.3. As the process of finalization of the revised Memorandum of Procedure (MoP) for appointment
of Judges to Supreme Court and High Courts was likely to take some time, on the initiative of the
Government of India the matter was taken up with the Supreme Court and the process of appointment
of Judges was resumed, so that administration of justice does not suffer pending finalization of the
revised MoP. Due to the combined efforts of the Government and Judiciary, during 2016, 126 fresh
appointments of Judges in High Courts which is the highest number of appointments made in a given
year. Besides, based on the proposal received from the Supreme Court Collegium, 4 Judges were
appointed in the Supreme Court in 2016. During the current year, as on date, 5 Judges have been
appointed in Supreme Court and 75 Judges have been appointed in High Courts.
13.4. The Judge strength of the Supreme Court (including the Chief Justice of India) is 31. As on
1.09.2017, 25 Judges are in position, leaving 6 vacancies of Judges to be filled. So far the Government
has not received any proposal for filling up the 06 vacant posts of Judges from the Supreme Court. As
on 1.09.2017 against the sanctioned strength of the High Court Judges of 1079, 666 Judges are in
position, leaving 413 vacancies of Judges to be filled. 135 proposals received from various High Courts
for filling up of vacancies are under various stages of process and proposals for remaining 278 vacancies
of Judges are awaited from the High Courts. Government is committed to filling up of vacancies in all
the High Courts. The observations/recommendations of Committee mentioned in 87th Report on Committee
on "Inordinate Delay in filling up vacancies in the Supreme Court and High Courts" have been noted and
are under consideration of Government and Judiciary.
Further Observation
13.5. The Committee appreciates the combined efforts of the Department and the Judiciary
which led to 126 fresh appointments of Judges in High Courts in the year 2016. However, a large
number of vacancies still exist in various High Courts. Accordingly, the Committee reiterates
that the Department should give effect to the recommendations of Committee in its Eighty-
seventh Report on "Inordinate Delay in filling up vacancies in the Supreme Court and High
Courts" and ensure that the vacancies in higher judiciary are filled up as soon as these arise
so that the justice delivery in the country is not hampered.
INCLUSIVENESS IN HIGHER JUDICIARY
Recommendation/Observation
14. The Committee also desires that the Bench of Higher Judiciary to be reflective of composition of
society and its diversity and recommends that suitable measures to include more and more people from
marginalized communities and women in the judiciary may be taken. (Para 6.32)

22
Action Taken
14.1. Appointment of Judges of the Supreme Court and High Courts is made under Articles 124 and
217 of the Constitution of India respectively. These Articles do not provide for reservation for any caste
or class of persons. The initiative of the proposal for appointment of Judges of Supreme Court and High
Courts vest with the Chief Justice of India/Supreme Court Collegium and Chief Justice/ High Court
Collegium respectively. If the Chief Minister desires to recommend the name of any person, he should
forward the name to the Chief Justice of the High Court for consideration. The Government has been
requesting the Chief Justices of the High Courts that while sending proposals for appointment of Judges,
due consideration be given to suitable candidates belonging to Scheduled Castes, Scheduled Tribes, Other
Backward Classes, Minorities and Women.
Further Observation
14.2. The Committee feels that in a diverse country like ours, inclusive and representative
judiciary will go a long way in instilling faith in the justice delivery system. Therefore, the
Committee reiterates the view taken in its Eighty-seventh Report on 'Inordinate delay in filling
up the vacancies in the Supreme Court and High Courts' that composition of higher judiciary
should reflect the diversity and composition of Indian society.
